She sends the correspondence concerning the Daughters of Saint Anne's request to run the "Saint Anne Home" and asks for his intervention to conclude the negotiations.

[Most Reverend Eminence,]

1. It is my duty to inform you of what is happening between the Administration of the home for old women, the "Saint Anne Home", and the Daughters of Saint Anne, who were waiting only to be called, for I had accepted according to their instructions; when they wrote asking me to send the conditions, I replied that I left it to their wisdom to set them.1

2. After this I believed everything was settled, when I received a letter from Cavaliere Matteucci, which I enclose together with our last reply and two others which I beg Your Most Reverend Eminence to read.2 Confidentially: one I received from Cav. Ugo Flandoli, through whom negotiations began, and the other was sent to Sig. G. B. Tornatore, our Superior. He replied maintaining that we (truly) not only had negotiations always in hand, but nothing stood between us and the Commission to prevent a definitive conclusion.

3. I commit this most delicate matter3 to Your Most Reverend Eminence's wisdom, and prostrate at your feet ask your Pastoral Blessing, remaining with veneration Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sister A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The matter had in fact taken a different turn, as appears from L 248, nn. 3-5.

2 Matteucci's letters are dated 8 and 12 December '80, and two others.

The latter have not survived.

She authorizes her to bring the postulants to Piacenza.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Come with the teacher and bring the certificates; come, and we will set the two of them right;2 tell the dear teacher that her father will be given not just 15 F. but 20, and even something more, and he will be very pleased3 and see many fine things.

Goodbye; everything in person your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves what she did about the postulant's board.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you that all you have done is well done, 1 for when you tell me they were owed to us, you have only done what duty requires.2 Certainly it takes money to keep someone, as you well know.3

Greetings to all; I wish you all a thousand good things in the heart of Jesus. I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She praises her for defending the Institute. Saint Anne will reward her by obtaining for her the Love of Jesus. Sadly someone is spreading slander against the Institute, discrediting it among the Daughters of Saint Anne themselves. But they, like you, have stood up to him.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter moved me deeply.2 Oh! you are a true daughter of my mother Saint Anne, for your heart is like hers. She is all love for her Institute, and when it is troubled she suffers! You, my dear daughter, who share so well in her sorrows, will surely be given a share in her graces by Saint Anne.

2. Oh! What are these graces, my dear daughter? To obtain for you the love of Jesus, in which lies all the good of heaven and earth!3 Oh! Love, to have You one must suffer, but this is sweet, for within it lies joy.4

3. Courage, daughter; the Lord's works grow only in tribulation, and so the work of the Holy Mother Saint Anne can have no other leaven than tribulation; to make it sharper He sends it through those whom the Institute has greatly benefited, like this man, who for some reason takes pleasure in going about whispering and disturbing my poor daughters.5

4. But by God's mercy he has found true and courageous pillars, hearts wholly consumed for their Institute, and yours is among them. When I come to Rome I will show you the letters and you will be amazed.6 I had yours delivered to him yesterday; I did not see him,7 for you must know that, as usual, on Christmas Day I was so ill I thought I would die, but no, and so yesterday I could hardly stand.

I still have a little trembling,8 from weakness; see how unsteady the pen is.

Goodbye; I am yours for ever and all ages, thanking you for your dear affection, and I remain once more your affectionate M. ROSA

The Child9 I enclose will tell you the rest.

She has received the letter and accounts. She always holds her close to the Heart of Jesus.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you I have received yours with the account.1 It is fine; so be cheerful, for your mother is better and always with you, holding you close, close to the heart of Jesus. Oh! sweet Love! Consume my dear daughter!

2. Have no doubt, [there is not] a moment when she does not think of her dear daughter.2 Thank you and all the Sisters for your good wishes; I greet them warmly and remain yours for all ages, affectionate M. ROSA

She insists that the Novices be sent with a Sister, entrusting to her the cash surplus. She will send good Sisters. Some money may be sent, addressed to the Consul or to her directly, to test whether it arrives.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hope you have received the registered letter I wrote on 10 Nov.,1 in which I repeated many things. Now I tell you that yours received, in which I hear you say that Father Rocchi will come to fetch the sisters.2

2. Oh! How it grieves me to see that you never answer what I tell you; moreover I would like you to tell me why you do this.

3. So I repeat that I want you to send me the money with Sr. A. Amadio and two or three novices, and I will send you other sisters well accompanied; do not doubt they will travel well. There is no need for Father Rocchi to come.3 But I tell you to send me all the money through the sisters.

4. Your letters make me laugh, for they always say the same things: that you have money, that you will send it, but nothing is seen; it is three years; the money Father Rocchi would spend you can give to the sisters, and so save it.4

5. So you did well to accept the pharmacy, but for pity's sake do not let the sisters overwork.

6. I urge you strongly and repeat that I would be sorry if this man came to fetch the Sisters.5 I do not know whether I would bring myself to hand them over, for I would like to send them by other means.

7. So [do not] fob me off any more, for to tell you what I think, it sounds like an old song. I will send you good Sisters, real angels. This year, as you will see from the circular, I have clothed 700, and last year 94. You see how it grows beyond measure. Ah! the Lord's goodness! How good He is!

8. You could try making a little packet and sending me a small amount to see whether it arrives safely, addressing it to the consul if you think fit, but try sending it here addressed to me. I see that where there is a will everything succeeds.6

Goodbye; I always write to you, and much more than you do,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Falsehoods and slanders have been hurled at the Institute. She mentions and refutes some of them. Her daughter Carlotta has never gone to the Institute's Houses since her marriage, and the same can be said of Alessandro. They have never appropriated the Institute's goods; had they done so, she would have been a thief and usurper of Saint Anne's property. These are rumors deliberately spread by someone who has been a beneficiary.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was a real comfort, for in it I saw first your good judgment, and secondly2 that the Saint has given you a heart like hers. Oh! how I thanked God!!

2. Yes, my dear! If God's goodness and mercy grant me life and strength to come, you will rejoice with me in person, facts in hand, to see in the full light of noon the falsehoods and slanders that wicked hearts hurl against our Mother Saint Anne,3 for they matter little to me, being dear Jesus' donkey. Donkeys feel nothing; they carry their load and care little or nothing.4

3. To the point: since her marriage my daughter has never gone round the houses; only once did she pass through Florence on her way from Rome, and another time she came with me to Lodi to buy things for herself in that city, and stayed out of the house the whole time with Sr. A. Benedetta.

4. Never, never did she go to the Daughters of Saint Anne; I would think those daughters should consider it an honor if my daughter deigned to visit them, and should kiss the ground she walks on, for through her they came into existence,5 and not a few sacrifices she had to make in her youth, sacrificing herself against her will, so that more than once she was seen crying because she did not want to be shut in and live a hard life, but for the Institute's sake she had to follow me; and many times, when she was little, I had to leave her with certain heartless Superiors, one of whom went so far as to slap her because she cried for her mamma; she wrote to me, and that Superior went to the post office and with a lie retrieved the letter,6 and seeing that she told me she was unhappy, that she was crying and wanted me to come and take her away, gave her two slaps. Oh! unheard-of cruelty!

5. Now they bring out these slanders. Oh! my Love! As for taking things. Oh! infernal lie, what is it saying? I will say that, were they not ill-bred, heartless and ungrateful, they should think it a happy omen if my daughter were kind enough to accept anything.7

6. But I ask: a person with a dowry like hers certainly cannot need our poor scraps;8 moreover, if the Daughters of Saint Anne had to give back to my children what I gave them, they could not do it, no; the accounts speak of it, the very walls say so, for they were bought with it.9

7. Oh! what am I saying? things I never wished to reveal until today, for I did not want my left hand to know what my right hand had done. But infamy forces me, to remove such a stain from the Institute (which is the apple of my eye), lest it remain that you, my dear daughters, had for Mother a thief, a usurper of the goods of the Holy Mother Saint Anne!10 Sweet suffering!

8. If my poor children had to write down what they suffered for your Institute, oh! pages would certainly be filled. My daughter keeps silent, but my son! You should hear him, and how he keeps on; the Sisters here could tell you something of what he did the last time he came!11

9. Enough; I will not dwell on this any longer. Let me tell you I have learned that you got many of these things from Father Alessandro; do you know why? He did the same wherever he went, for my dear daughters who truly love their Institute have written to me about what he went about spreading, but he received some fine rebukes.12

10. Tell me, did he say nothing to you? This friar has received immense benefits from us, and that is how the world goes! May all be praise to God, who gives us the means to atone for my enormous sins. All for Him alone and nothing for me.

11. Holy Cross, beautiful Cross, sweet Love who dwells only in dear suffering! So take great heart, and let everyone do as they think, for they serve only as instruments enabling us to do a little good and gain the beautiful dwelling of Paradise.13

Goodbye; greetings to you all; pray for me; and ever for all ages your affectionate M. ROSA

She will send two Sisters. Let her keep her spirits up and write what she needs. Encouragement.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You complain that I do not write. My God! There is so much going on! Anyway, I tell you I always hold you close to the Heart of Jesus!

2. I hope two good, strong sisters will reach you by the end of the week; be a little patient.

3. Sr. A. Berarda2 writes that she left everything in order, left the provisions well stocked and gave you money, didn't she? According to her all was going well.

4. Keep your spirits up, for we shall see each other soon; if you lack anything write to me and I will send you what you need. I repeat: keep your spirits up, and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

She hears all is going well. She has tried to satisfy her by sending a Sister.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say in your letter, and am delighted to hear you found everything in order. As for the servants, let us trust in the Lord.2

2. So from the telegram you will have seen that I have fully satisfied you. She soprano (?) well; in short, you will find her a good sister in every way.3

3. I would like to tell you many things, but I am so overwhelmed with work that I do not know how. Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

She does not agree that Father Rocchi should come to Italy to fetch more Sisters. She repeats that she has written several times that a sister should come with two Novices. Worried that her letters are not arriving, she sends this one to the Bishop. Let her accept requests to open other houses; more Sisters will be sent.1

A.M.F

My daughter,

1. It pains me greatly to hear that you prefer to send Father Rocchi rather than a sister; I certainly deplore it! What, before you were so opposed to him and now you have made him your missionary?2

2. I cannot understand how my letters go astray, for a year now I have done nothing but write the same thing: send a Sister with two Novices and I will send you others; but you never answer on this point.3

3. I keep saying you can send Sr. A. Amadio, who I hear is unwell,4 and you can safely trust her with what you have; but this too will go astray. Either you do not receive them or you do not answer to the point. What am I to think? I register them, I change the address, and nothing ever comes of it;5 I am sending this one to the Bishop to see whether even through him they get lost. I would like to know what to do; I would not want someone here to be intercepting them.

4. I repeat that you are not to send the fur to the Bishop of Piacenza, no, but to our Cardinal Protector,6 to whom I wrote that you should write, as the other Sisters have done; I even enclosed a draft so that you could copy it and send it to him.7

5. I do not know; I have always written each sister a letter of encouragement; in short, I tell you I fear they are being taken there, and my fears rest on something real. So I tell you to complain and find out where it comes from. I believe it is R.8 Ah! If only it were not! But! Anyway, now I shall see about this one. If this goes astray, I will certainly find out how things stand, for with a friend of the Daughters of Saint Anne I will find a way.

6. So I hope all I tell you will be carried out, and then things will certainly go better; moreover I know other cities ardently want us, but they approached Father Rocchi and he is the one who stopped it, for he wants to be the one who does everything; besides, this time I am not using that person to send you this letter but someone else;9 I will do so as soon as I reach Rome, where I will learn more.

7. So do what I tell you and you will certainly be pleased; look into these towns that are eager to have the sisters; I fear they will take the Sisters of Charity.10 So get moving and accept; I will then send the Sisters.

Goodbye; greetings to all the Sisters; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She sends a Sister for the laundry and linen room and will obtain the document requested.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I gather from your telegram that you want a laundress; but not actually to wash, for we supervise the laundry but do not do it ourselves; that is how it is done in all the hospitals and orphanages we run;2 it is not at all fitting; so, for pity's sake.

2. You will see that Sr. A. Desideria will do well, for she irons well. Here she was always the one in charge, and in Rome too; and for the linen room she is excellent. Sr. A. Carla is no good and has no strength; she is clumsy in doing things; in short, she is not capable.3

3. I am glad to hear you have already begun, and as for the sister's certificate I will do all I can, though we cannot go; it is a...4 anyway, in haste,

your affectionate M. ROSA

A call to gratitude to the Lord. News: the holy death of 14 Sisters; the blessed fruits of their motherly charity, shown in sinners returning to God's heart; the opening of 12 houses; the clothing of 100 postulants. The Holy Father continues to show his esteem and has appointed Cardinal Gaetano Alimonda as Protector. These spiritual fruits are granted by God as a reward for our filial love of Mother Saint Anne, who lives in her true daughters with the energy that kindles them with God's holy love. Advice on observance.1

A.M.F.

Circular letter [Dearly beloved daughters],

1. Casting our eyes, dearly beloved Daughters, over the whole of this year eighteen hundred and eighty now ending, we have reason to exclaim with the Holy Prophet: "O Lord my God, for ever will I sing Your divine mercies"1

2. The most signal of these mercies is that so many of our sisters have been crowned with the crown of eternal happiness. Sisters, this is the whole purpose and gain for which God placed us in the Family of our Holy Mother: He placed us there so that, through the care, solicitude and protection she lavishes on us from Heaven, we might live as her true daughters, observing her Rules, and so learn to die well, that is, to die in it the precious death of the just, and then be precious jewels in her crown in Heaven.2

3. Now we have every reason to hold as certain that our merciful God has granted this mercy to no fewer than 14 sisters.3

Yes, they died a death that leaves nothing to be desired, the best assurance that they are in Heaven enjoying God in the company of the Holy Mother.

4. Not [only] the good but even the wicked have been obliged to pay tribute to their charity, which, in imitation of their Divine Master, drove them to sacrifice their bodily life to relieve their neighbor.4

5. To their motherly charity towards the sick, Jesus Christ granted the consolation of leading many back to His loving divine heart,5 after long years in which they had abandoned Him, given themselves to the devil and were on the point of eternal damnation.

6. Among these converted sinners was a Protestant heretic; nursed by our Sisters at the end of his life, and seeing the truly Christian charity with which they cared for him night and day, he recognized that the Roman Church, which can inspire so disinterested a love of neighbor, could only be the Church of Jesus Christ; so, moved by divine grace, he publicly abjured his errors and was converted, and in their arms passed holily to Paradise, as we may hope.

7. Ah! Sisters, with how many souls the Institute's charity crowns the Holy Mother's throne and has peopled holy Paradise!6 But hold fast to this, sisters: all these spiritual fruits that God grants are the reward of the filial love we bear the Holy Mother, august and venerable Mother of the Immaculate.7

8. She lives in her true Daughters; and so if her true Daughters are able to keep their hearts free of attachment to possessions, pleasures and honors, they will be kindled with God's holy love, be holy themselves and sanctify their neighbor.

9. So the longing to become truly loving Daughters of our Holy Mother must always be alive,8 honoring her with all the daily devotions the Institute has established for this purpose, and spurring them on by faithful observance of the Holy Rules.

10. It is their emblem as Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of Mary

Immaculate, Mother of God, that makes them objects of admiration and veneration in the eyes of the people, so that from all sides come requests for new Houses. This year twelve new ones have been opened;9 but how many more requests could not be accepted for lack of personnel.

11. It is true that this year we clothed a hundred Postulants, yet for so many Houses they are few. Let us pray, Sisters, that Divine Providence may provide this Mother House with means, so that we can receive the many who ask to be admitted to the Institute but, given the times, cannot provide the small dowry required.

12. The Holy Father continues to show his fatherly esteem and affection for our company. At the beginning of the year he graciously received us in audience and with great kindness spent a long time with us, having us sit in his presence. He was pleased to assign us Cardinal Gaetano Alimonda as protector,10 a Cardinal who shines like a sun in the Sacred College for virtue and wisdom alike. He shows great solicitude and energy for the good of the Institute.

13. The Bishops, too, never cease to rejoice with us at the fruits of blessing the sisters bring to their Dioceses.

14. But again we repeat that [it is] the most powerful protection of the Holy Mother before the throne of God most high11

15. Now we shall urge on you the observance of the chief points of our Holy Rules, which will make you ever dearer to the heart of the Holy Mother:

1. Punctual observance of the timetable from morning to night, for devotions well performed make us good before God.

2. We exhort Superiors to treat the Sisters in their care, in food and clothing, just as they are treated here in the Mother House. When the Sisters have the food they need, they have the strength to carry out their duties well, work willingly, shun idleness, the father of all vices, and are not tempted to grumble; but the Sisters too are bound to be content; when they are healthy they must love the common life.

3. Superiors must watch that there are no particular friendships in their Houses, seeing that the Sisters keep the rules, which forbid them to touch one another even slightly, this being the means of keeping such friendships away. And where there are no such friendships, the heavenly virtue of chastity is safe among them.

4. We exhort, beg and implore that they never speak alone with persons of the opposite sex, in accordance with the Rules. And in this let the Superiors lead by example. Woe to anyone guilty of breaking these Rules! They are the safeguard of chastity towards outsiders and of the reputation, before the whole world, of being Angels clothed in flesh.12

16. We trust, dearly beloved Daughters, that you will receive these words as dictated by the immense love we bear for your spiritual and temporal good, so as to see you all holy, that one day we may all rejoice together in our triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and in our Savior Jesus Christ, beside the throne of our Mother Mary Immaculate and of our Holy Mother, the glorious Saint Anne

GIOVANNI BATT. TORNATORE Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

XShe hopes this letter and the registered packet of letters will arrive. By obedience she must send the Sister and the Novices.1

1. I hope this one will not suffer the fate of last year's;2 I will send it in a packet by safe hands.

2. What can I say? Only repeat that I want two novices and that you send me the savings; I would much prefer a sister to come and fetch the others you want; but if that does not happen I will not give any Sisters.3

3. You know that I live by obedience, and so the daughters of the Holy Mother Saint Anne must be truly obedient. So do as I tell you and you will surely be well loved by the Saint. I do not want to doubt your obedience, nor that I will soon have what I desire.

4. I have sent another of these circulars by a safe route, and other letters through the Bishop, which I hope you will receive safely, and another registered packet containing all the letters for the Sisters; if it goes astray I have the receipt and will claim it.4

5. Courage, for it is time to work and suffer so as one day to have the good fortune of being held close to dear Jesus. Love much and you will be blessed!

[your affectionate M. ROSA]

She insists again that she send a Sister and the Novices and hand over the savings. She urges a uniform religious habit.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Once again I receive a letter of yours, dated 2 November. My God! What stabs to this poor breast! Oh! Daughter, are you disobeying me? That is certainly why you can never have God's blessing!

2. What, for a year I have been writing to you to send two Novices and a Sister — the one I hear has heart trouble — who would bring all the money you have,1 and you keep fobbing me off saying you have no one to send it with? And now you send me Fr Rocchi!2 Oh! What wounds on every side! I will send you nothing, neither Sisters nor what you ask.3

3. I see well that you are making fun of me, and certainly the Holy Mother Saint Anne will not help you. For a year now I have kept on at you to send what I say above.

4. I hope this year you have received the circulars, and from them you can gather how much I have to do and the enormous expenses; our budget for the Mother House alone amounts [to] £ 74,000, seventy-four thousand.

5. Can you see where it has come from?4 Not from the Superiors,5 for a poor mother who can no longer travel round because of her grave illnesses — two bouts of bronchitis already this winter, but!6 — and they left me so weak I cannot stand. There are days when I can hardly keep on my feet, and yet I must travel with a thousand torments. Oh! What sorrows, my dear daughter!

6. Certainly if your eyes could see me you would have pity, and yet a rain of sorrows surrounds me; I assure you they are beyond compare. I feel them bending the back of this donkey, weakened to the extreme.7

7. Pray hard for me, as I pray for you every day. I do not leave church in the morning without first commending you to God, even in my illnesses, during which by God's mercy I have always been able to receive Holy Communion, though unworthily.8 For 25 years, by God's mercy, I have never missed it.

8. Oh! Heart of my Jesus, how good You are! I truly feel all the gratitude and Love shown to so unworthy and wretched a creature as I am. Oh! Dear Jesus! So think seriously and try to obey.

9. I had told you to see that our habit was restored there too, but instead I see you continue to wear white, which displeases me very, very much. So it is time we were all the same; it seems to me that everything can be achieved when one wants it.

Greetings to all the Sisters; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks her to help a Sister in the School. She will send the books.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Be patient if I do not write, for I have so much to do! And besides I am about to leave. I commend the sister to you; do what you can; it seems to me one could say you should help her because she is shy, couldn't one?2

2. As for the books, as soon as I am in Ferrara I will send them; be patient.3 One day we will talk about many things in person. Love Jesus greatly, so as to be consumed; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She encloses the circular letter.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the circular; you will see how much there is to do.1 Greetings to all, and believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is glad to hear she is in good health and asks for prayers for her coming journey.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was most comforting; God be blessed that at last good air has been found for your health, and a Superior who is a mother to you.2

2. Pray for me, for I am about to set out;3 if God gives me strength I will certainly come to you; tell the Superior not to write unless there is something important, for I will not be settled in Naples until the end of February, God willing.

Yours for ever,

affectionate M. ROSA

Tomorrow I will send what the Superior asked for4

She asks for two recommendations: for reduced railway fares and for a duplicate of a lost document.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, see whether you can get a letter of recommendation to Mancini in Rome; I really need it, so that I can apply for half fares in the Romagna.2 Speak to Fr Francesco about it; tell him I am counting on him.3

2. One more thing you must say: here in Piacenza we have a very bad inspector, first because he cannot abide religious orders and then because if a certificate is lost he will not even issue an attestation. We have a sister who has lost her certificate, and his answer was that since she lost it he will not give it again. What do you think of that? And [to] another, who will be one of our sisters [in a] few days, he sent it at once because he did not know she was to be a nun.4

3. What do you think? Is it not sheer caprice? So tell Fr Francesco to see how he can be transferred, and meanwhile tell me what to do;5 and meanwhile send me letters for Mancini; send everything here and the Superior will forward them to me.6 Goodbye. A thousand good wishes in the heart of Jesus; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letter. Words of affection and desires for holiness in intimate union in the Heart of Jesus.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received yours and hear first of all, to my great comfort, that you are all in good health; all I can tell you is that today my head seems willing to give me a little respite; yesterday I suffered all day.

2. For your information, I will stay here until Saturday; I have received only two letters, one from you and the other from Onorata; with the telegram I received one, and nothing more.2

3. Oh! My dear Daughter, why do you speak of forgiveness?!3 Oh! Come, you must not think of such things, but only that your poor mother bears you a great affection, such that only dear Jesus could show you its measure!

4. Oh! Enough to say that I want you holy, and when this is nourished in the soul one must always be held close to the Heart of Jesus our Love.4 Love is inventive; it seeks nothing but to please the beloved; and our Beloved desires nothing but to be loved. So we must try everything to make Him loved and served by the whole world.

5. So, my daughter, the moral is this: wanting you holy, that one day you might come to sanctify the whole world!5

6. I hear about the dinners; I did not doubt it, for my departure will have gladdened the hearts of both, and certainly what should have been held back for... now freely and at length they do what they think is for the good of the Institute.6

7. I think I have found the Superior for the Crotone hospital; I am sending her from here.

Goodbye, for I have so much to do; believe me yours; you know, grandmother is ill; have prayers said. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

News of her health and travels.

Dear children,

1. A line from me too to tell you I am fairly well and suffered little on the journey; perhaps I will stay here until Saturday and then [in] Pisa until Monday.1 I commend the little girls to you, and please see to the matter of conscience.2 The climate here is very mild. It was curious: the snow accompanied us from Bologna as far as Piteccio; before the tunnel there was a good half-span of snow; after the tunnel everything changed: mild air, no snow, the moon. Oh! What a surprise! Carla will be busy with the new maid, won't she?

Greetings to you both, and a big kiss to the little girls; believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA. Dear Nonny, be happy, for I will bring you lots of lovely things.3

Advice concerning the School in via della Morte.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear the teacher does not teach as she should; well, I have written to the M. to change her as he pleases, but it is not advisable to put the novice there, for she would be lost. It is better to let him change the teacher.2

2. If you have no money write to me, or better, telegraph at once and I will reply by telegram. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks her to tell Fr Francesco she has acted on his advice and to thank him.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Tell Fr Francesco that I have received his letter; I thank him very much and have at once written to the Sister to send me all the particulars he asks for.2 With God's help I will try to be in Rome by the 23rd of this month; tell him, and it will be a real pleasure if I can see the deputy Farina and receive his visit.

2. Oh! If Mancini takes it up,3 we will certainly get everything the Sisters of Charity have had! Thank him warmly for me; tell him that if I can be of service in anything he has only to ask; and believe me ever your affectionate M. ROSA

Various instructions about the Sisters and the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Two Sisters will reach you: Sr. A. Corinna and Sr. A. Pacifica; keep one, Sr. A. Corinna, and send Sr. A. Pacifica back with another.1 If one could trust her to do well, the one with the machine could be sent; what do you think?2

2. I hear about Sr. A. Michelina. Listen, do not send her any more, for pity's sake; I will tell you why in person; and tell Gaspare that for good reasons I do not think it right for her to go there;3 I will write to him myself.

3. I hear some debts have come up,4 but the one of £ 100 has been paid, and the other too; I gave the money to Gaspare and you will see they are already entered.

4. Please buy 4 meters of oilcloth5 to send to Arena Po. Tomorrow morning I leave for Rome and will write to them from there. The Lord bless you.

Affectionate M. ROSA

Greetings to Gaspare and Carla.

They will have letters from me from Rome straight away.

She is to send two Sisters and organize the running of the house before leaving.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter asks where you are to send the one with the machine. With Sr. A. Pacifica, back to Appignano; have I made myself clear?2

2. Dear Francesca, before you leave it is best to leave everything in order and locked up.

3. For expenses, tell Francesco and leave him about 100 Fr.; he is to note everything down, not waste any, make it last, and if he runs out, tell the Superior you leave behind.3 Tell her not to spend any postulants' money if any arrive,4 understood?

4. Enough; Jesus will help you, I am sure of it; I always tell Him so, and in Him I hold you close; in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

As for Sr. A. Olga's mother, who asks to enter the Institute, she should hear the Parish Priest's opinion. Care with money; attend to observance and the service of the sick.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about Sr. A. Olga's mother. She is very insistent on being clothed and would then come here to see to her property.2 Ask the Parish Priest; what does he say?

2. As for the money, it seems to me the others should have contributed too; for pity's sake be careful what you do, do not waste it, but 40 Fr. seems too much for the valuation;3 I add only that I commend observance and the poor sick to you.

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters; pray for me, your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves what she has done and asks for news. Various advice. She has worked hard; her health has recovered but she is still weak.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Everything the Father had you do is fine.2 I hope you have sent Sr. A. Pacifica off with the one with the machine.3

2. You tell me nothing about the little girls' health, nor Carla's and Gaspare's, and I am very sorry. For pity's sake tell me the truth about how they are; and you say nothing about that witch of a Marchioness.4

3. As for clothing Olga's mother, it seems to me she could be clothed;5 as for what she says, I would not know what to say.

4. I hear about the letters; I have read them and would not know what to say. Listen, do what Jesus inspires you.6 My God, I do not know what to say!

Dear Francesca, oh! how many sorrows! Pray and have others pray for me; believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

5. I am reopening the letter to tell you I have received your telegram. In strict confidence, I am a little better, but the cough!7

It is late, eleven at night; I have had a lot of work, being many days behind;8 I am very weak! Let us hope the worst is over; do not worry. I would like to know what day you have set for the clothing;9 tell me lots of things when you write. You will already have received another letter of mine, haven't you? And Gaspare too; I commend the little girls to you; pray and [...]10

She may accept the teacher and, if she is willing to go to one of our houses even outside Piacenza, send her at once.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter says you wish you could give me something as the others do, and that they all give me something!!! Oh!! Enough! Jesus for me, and that is all.2

2. As for the teacher, I accept her; but I would want her to be willing to go with us, even outside Piacenza.3 If she agrees, send her to Piacenza straight away, so that meanwhile she can teach the novices. Send her to Piacenza at once.

3. Thank you, and Fr Francesco too, to whom I will write soon,4 for I am still unwell. Goodbye; greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to accept the three postulants and have them taken to Piacenza, and give the money to the Superior Francesca to bring to Rome. It is needed to buy two houses.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours; in haste: accept all three postulants; send the money here and send them to Piacenza, but wait, for a Sister returning to Piacenza will come and take them.2

2. But once they are accepted, it is good to have them come at once; if this sister is late, you can take them yourself, and if you could stay there 15 days, so that the Superior Francesca could come here, for she is to bring me Sr. A. Michelina.3

3. So see whether you can go. Ask Sr. A. Eletta whether she will manage; I will write to her; tell her and write to me at once.4

4. Give the postulants' money to the Superior Francesca to bring me; let her keep it in her bosom,5 say nothing, and bring me plenty, for I must pay the rent6 and try to raise enough to buy the houses in Naples and Florence, about which I have written to the lawyer.

5. I hope he will reply; write to me at once. I am a tiny bit better, but extremely weak! Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

News of her health. She is waiting for her so they can go to Naples together.

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca,

1. In reply to yours of today: I think we should not get involved with that man, no, because...1 Write to the Superior of Cortemaggiore to look for another, or else we will find a woman; let that man not be mentioned again.

2. My health is a little better; thank you for your prayers, but I really thought... anyway, I have been up for 3 days; say nothing; a very bad cough caught in Pistoia; how I suffered! Today I have coughed little.

3. Listen, I have just finished writing to Sr. A. Santina to come and relieve you for about 15 days, leaving Sr. A. Eletta in her place, for I truly found she does well; she will give you things to bring me.2

4. Since I cannot go out — it is snowing, it is cold and I fear a relapse — I still have everything to do; I have not even asked for the address; I have no strength; I am extremely weak from the blistering plasters!!

5. Today I was lucky enough to get a little decoction; I have great hopes of it. As for Nonny, I would say no, for how could we manage? If they all came, well and good, but she alone!3

What am I to do? And then! Enough.

6. As soon as you come with Sr. A. Michelina we will leave for Naples, and then, well, I will stay in Naples 15 days and then off again. I hope to be home by the end of February.

7. Oh! But say nothing about my illness, which thank God is over; now I must set to work on the painful and distressing business of the wretched Arnedos.4

Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

Alarmed by bad news of Rosetta's health, she suggests remedies. Advice for Carlotta and Nonny too.

A.M.F.

My children,

1. Last night when I read yours, I assure you it hurt me deeply to hear poor Rosette is still ill. It is time she was better, and I assure you I am terribly anxious at the thought that she may go into consumption; the thought torments me.1 Oh! Poor child! I remember that, with that cough, she was taken out of the warm room and sent downstairs for her milk. What harm would there have been in her having it in the room?2 Oh! How careful one must be with little ones!

2. Write at once to Signora Maddalena3 to send you a little decoction suitable for the child, without losing time; a small poultice on the stomach, its juice pressed out on perforated brown paper;4 and always good broth. For pity's sake do not neglect her! I hear you left her alone at home while you took Nonny to the theater. Oh! In this cold! Be careful, light the fire.5 I am worried.

3. Carla, if I find her poorly I will turn round and leave; I want to find her plump; so you must eat and be cheerful, and Rosette must not be crossed in anything; do not make her cry.

Let Nonny be cheerful, for I shall soon be back and will not leave her again; she will always come with me; bring her to meet me at Parma and we will go to Piacenza together; I want them both, poor little things!

4. As for the lawyer, I have done everything from here; nothing more is needed; for pity's sake do not make out any receipt, even if the law yer says so.6 You will hear why in person.

5. It is terribly cold here, snow and rain; I imagine it is the same in Piacenza. Look after the little ones. Carla is not to go to the theater; she must keep well wrapped up.

Kisses to the little girls, a handshake to you both; I am ever

Affectionate M. ROSA

She will send the cook. Advice about some Sisters and the organization of the work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You are right that I did not reply; there are two reasons: first, I was ill; second, there was nothing in your letters that needed an answer. Now here I am.

2. You want a cook; I will send one at once, but do not expect that someone who must cook well can also be a giant; she will be capable and economical; there you are.1 As for the wage, leave it as the maid's is, for it does not do to look too tight-fisted; what do you think? Since she will have her board, she will certainly economize for you too.2 So leave it like that; when you write I will send her.

3. I am extremely pleased with dear Olga! Oh! If the Lord hears my prayers she will be perfectly well.3 For pity's sake she must not remove the issue; let her keep it always open, for it will be her health. And if the thing has come back!! Oh! She is cured!

4. As for the play, since you know the Archbishop is pleased, I am delighted.4

Yes, try to get rid of all the lay staff, so that order will take root and it will become a true educational establishment.

5. Kiss the Archbishop's hand for me and believe me yours; greet ing all the sisters, tell Sr. A. Giuditta that I have received her letter and have written at once to obtain her certificate. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. It would be good for you to stop writing to Pisa5 and give up all your correspondence there; this is my wish.

Instructions and advice concerning a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you are unwell; I too have been ill, but am better now.1 Oh! What are you telling me about Sr. A. del Crocifisso!2 For pity's sake she must never go near the girls, no; keep her well away from them and punish her severely; forbid her to go into the kitchen or anywhere else. How dreadful!3

2. What is to be done? My God! I really do not know what to say; how is she with her illness?4

I am writing her a couple of lines. Goodbye; greetings to all; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letters and expects her with the Sister and the Father. She needs money to conclude the business in hand. She asks for prayers.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you want the letters; I need to look for them; meanwhile you can reply if you remember; I really have no time.2 Today I went out and tomorrow, God willing, I will go out again; think how immense the work is and how little strength I have.3

2. Your two letters, one last night and one this morning, were a great comfort, telling me you are all well; but I would like to know why the Father telegraphed that he is coming on Monday and you with Michelina;4 it is better with the Father, so that you are accompanied. Meanwhile I am not yet ready; anyway, as soon as you receive this, telegraph or write the exact day you will come, and I will then telegraph Sr. A. Santina to come;5 and if the Father is coming, telegraph me; but I expect you all together. So tell me something.

3. Hold the clothing, for it is needed;6 otherwise all you have done is fine. Bring all, all the money, for I must buy... you will see.

4. I am searching everywhere for money to carry out this transaction.7

Dear Francesca, what trials there are when one has to deal with certain people; I really do not know what to think! Sr. A. Santina will bring postulants and give you the dowry; bring that too,8 in short everything, for I need far more. Oh! What a tangle! May God give me strength to bear it all!9 You will hear in person.

5. So you will certainly be with me with Sr. A. Michelina within a week at the latest. Tell her I am not writing because I am too busy; so pray and have others pray. Tell Sr. A. Basilia to make a novena to the Holy Mother entirely for me, for I need it, and the baker Sr. A. Rosaria to pray and obtain from Our Lady what I need so much.10

Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks her to bring some things and to telegraph the day of departure.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I wrote today, and tonight, late as it is, a line; it is 11 o'clock and I am tired. The Father tells me about the lawyer business.1 Oh! If you had telegraphed me, I would have told you how and where to get the money, rather than turning to that viper!2

2. Listen, when you come bring me two habits' worth of cloth, that is, still to be made up, and a little salami and luganeghini.3 In today's telegram you say nothing about coming with the Father; I no longer understand anything.

3. Write the exact day you leave, so that I have time to telegraph Sr. A. Santina to come there.4

4. I am a little better; the cough has almost gone. I am going to bed, for I feel cold coming on. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She will have to stay in Rome a long time, so it is better to postpone her coming to Rome; she will let her know. She asks for the register of postulants and a Sister's letters. News.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, do me the kindness of sending me by the Father all of Arnedos's letters, and that of her cousin Baron Lupinacci; tell me how long a postulancy she did. How dreadful!1

2. You can thank the Bishop warmly for the fine recommendations he gave me when he came to Rome. I hear, and for this I shall have to stay here a good while,2 so as I cannot go to Naples there is no point in your coming, nor Sr. A. Michelina.3

3. You will come as soon as I see I can be ready; I will write 'come', and Sr. A. Santina will come to relieve you, as arranged; but I do not think I will have you come so soon, for since I must stay here a long time yet, it is better for you to wait in Piacenza.

4. I have not yet asked for the audience,4 only because I am very weak, but I have climbed enough stairs already. I will wait for you for the audience.

5. Have prayers said for the Arnedos matter, which is really serious.5

6. It is spring-warm here; I hope God will temper the cold there too.

I have sent you the letters of obedience6 signed, and today [I have] received those you sent me. Goodbye; love to Carla,

your affectionate M. ROSA

7. You have done everything well. Send me the postulants' book in which the dowries are recorded; give it to the Father; keep them noted in a rough book and they can be copied out later.7

She has heard she is unwell and asks for news of her and the children. News of Alessandro and others.

A.M.F.

Dear Carlotta,

1. I hear you are not too well; what is the matter? Why are you not eating? Cheer up, for I am getting through things as fast as I can to come home. I will stay in Naples only a very short time; so if you want me to come soon and bring you a lovely present, I want to hear that you are eating well, are cheerful and putting on weight; then you will see what Mamma will do.

2. Now I want to make you laugh: Alessandro and Maria came to see me for two days and went straight back to their house at Alatri.1

3. Do you want to laugh? Sr. A. Benedetta noticed that Maria smokes and drinks like a porter — 4 or 5 of those big stemmed glasses full of wine without water. Oh! How funny! You will hear in person. The boy seems half... big, big, but from the knocks he gets he seems dim; it is comical; you will hear. Maria said he does not eat. Ah! What tales! He is fat as a capon!

4. It seems a hundred years since I saw you; take care of yourself; write and tell me whether you are eating and cheerful. Oh! Are Nonny and Nonnetto well? Why do you tell me nothing?

5. The Duchess of Sora2 came to see me yesterday with her husband; she sends greetings to you and Gaspare, as does the Marchioness Cavalletti; poor creature! How sorry I am for her!3 I wish you could see something of other people's troubles; oh! yours would seem nothing. Kiss the dear little girls, and my love to Gaspare; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

There has been a misunderstanding about collecting the Mass money. Only the receipt is to be sent to her; the money goes to Canon Fantini.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Thank you for your kind heart in wanting to send me something; keep it all, for by God's mercy I do not need it; I need prayers to bear the great sorrows and tribulations that weigh on me. Oh! Accinelli!!!1 May the Lord give him a thousand blessings.

2. Listen, I am truly hurt to hear from the Superior of Genoa that she says I wrote to you to send me the Mass money as soon as you had collected it. Ah! What nonsense!

3. Listen, I told Sr. A. Benedetta that you and the Superior of Genoa are to go and collect it, then you will give the money to the Superior and return the paper to me, for good order, since papers must be kept at the Mother House.2

4. And the Superior of Genoa must give this money to Canon Fantini — theirs is the Sunday Mass.3 How dreadful! Does she think I want to pocket the Mass money? Shall I eat it!? Shall I give it away? Oh! Dear Felicita, I am overwhelmed with sorrows! Suffering, you are sweet to me!!4

Goodbye; pray for me and have others pray for me!

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She is ready to send another Sister and explains the conditions: the fare must be paid.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear the Archbishop wants another sister. I am ready, but he must send me the travel money; I have to take her from Piacenza, so you see one alone cannot come; he must pay for two,1 or else wait at least a month, when some sisters are due to go there, that is to Aci Catena, and she can go with them.

2. If you need one, you can take one of the nurses temporarily;2 tell the Archbishop; and whether he is happy to wait or would have me send two, tell me what to do.

Otherwise what you tell me is fine; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

The Marchioness has no right to complain. She urges patience over the postponement of her journey to Rome. Various errands.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear from your letter that that wretched Marchioness, after receiving so much good, has the nerve to complain.1 Jesus was betrayed by one of His apostles whom He had benefited so much; I make this meditation in practice, for these days dear Jesus is giving me a share in that same sorrow!2

2. Be patient if you do not come with Sr. A. Michelina now; what can I do, I am held captive here and perhaps for a good while!! So I have not even asked for the audience; I am waiting to reach the end of so many martyrdoms, and then, when I ask for the audience, I will telegraph you to leave, and at the same time Sr. A. Santina will arrive.3

3. Send me more letters of obedience to sign.4 As soon as you have money, give 450 to the lawyer and 500 to Gaspare. If the Lord hears me you will certainly have everything.5

4. See whether you can find the contract for this house in Rome; in the contracts pigeonhole there is also the contracts folder.6

I have written to the lawyer directly; have these accounts entered in the book. Take care of the books, which may have to be inspected.7

5. Oh! Dear Francesca, what one has to see of the barbarity of men! And the malice! I am getting all the permits ready to visit the relics, so that as soon as you arrive you can see everything.8 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She has relieved her of a burden by taking on the absent teacher's work; it is hard to find a replacement so late in the school year. That house always has health problems.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. Your letter has, I can truly say, eased my mind a little: for now I need not send the teacher. Oh! A thousand blessings on you!1 Not everyone realizes what a tangle it is to find a teacher now when they are all at work; one cannot pull one parish apart to patch up another, nor easily find one.2 Ah! What a blessed house! There is always something!

2. Do you see Sr. A. Olga? If you saw how well she is! It is a real joy;3 I hope this other one will recover too; with these people they are all consumptive,4 but how is it that this last one never had anything wrong while she was with us!5 Anyway, my sins turn everything upside down. Pray for me.

3. Have you received the shawl and overcoat? I know they were sent.

4. Tell your client6 that I will think about what she had written to me, but she must be at peace, think of being good and not grumble, above all!!7

Ah! How they love telling tales about the house, ah!

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters, and believe me ever, for all ages, your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves the votive offering to Saint Anne and urges prayer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yes, I allow you to take the votive offering to the Saint; I join you with all my heart in making it.1 As for the Sister, oh! yes, we must pray hard for her. May God convert her for us.2 I will write about the certificate.

Let us pray hard; Jesus will help us, your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received their letters and asks for more news of the granddaughters. She has sent oil for the house.1

A.M.F.

My son, dearest Carla,

1. I have received your two letters, which were very dear to me, telling me you are well and Rosetto better; and my dear Nonny? What is she doing? Ah! If only I could fly to you! But I am made of lead, so patience is needed. It is really very warm here; and in Piacenza? I am always worried about the little girls.2

2. Listen, I have sent 110 liters; they put your address on it, but it is for the house; it is very good.3 I will have more sent for the lamps, which is very cheap.4 You must keep the receipts when the railway papers arrive, for when the barrels have to be returned it costs less.

3. The lamp oil I cannot send for lack of money! Oh! What scarcity! Frightful, and it is the same everywhere.5 Well, the Lord's will be done! Well done, Carla, keep strong and you will be my consolation; my dear Nonny, and Rosetto too. Warm greetings, and believe me, you two, yours,

affectionate M. ROSA

Read it as best you can; it is late and I can no longer see for tiredness.

She reassures her about the previous letter and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply by return of post. How can I possibly have used such harsh words as to distress you? My God! You know whether it ever entered my mind; rather I thought I was confiding in you about the Genoa one and the Masses.1

2. In any case, for pity's sake, do not be upset. Yes! Yes! I have had too many proofs of your affection. God reward you, dear daughter.

3. What days of tribulation! My God! Pray and have others pray; one day, if it please the good God, you will hear in person.2 Truly suffering is sweet, above all when it is without comfort.

4. You tell me nothing about the teacher, nor about the one for Sestri, which is a serious matter. Try to find one with a lower-grade certificate.3 I have spoken with Farina; thank Fr Francesco.4

Goodbye; it is late and I am tired; yours for all ages

affectionate M. ROSA

She is not pleased with her conduct. She must treat the Sisters with charity and try to amend.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am very sorry to have to tell you that I am not at all pleased with your way of acting. So a little more charity towards the sisters, poor things; otherwise it gives rise to discontent and grumbling.2

2. So, in haste, I tell you I would not want you to torment the sisters because of this admonition. Woe!3 Instead you must amend and take care to amend.4

Sure of obtaining everything, I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She explains how to deal with a novice who is leaving the Institute. Advice, news; she asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

1. In reply to your letter and telegram: for your guidance, I have written to the Bishop setting out the account: she1 brought £ 320 and we keep 150 for the clothing, one franc a day for two months of postulancy and a year of Novitiate; that makes 255 for us, which you will deduct from the cloth she says she brought.

2. I am sending this account to the Bishop, and you will give her the same, properly drawn up, and tell her: "Go to His Excellency by all means; he will certainly say nothing, being intelligent enough not to be persuaded otherwise".2

3. I am sending you two letters: one, you will see, concerns two postulants; not the old one, but yes to the young one; tell Signor Baratelli of S. Lazzaro.3 As for the other, I do not know who she is, but she has evidently already been accepted, so write and tell her to come at once.

4. As for the sisters [who] are to come, I will write and tell you whom to send.

5. Well, oh! you long to see me, and what about me? Enough; it is a year now that if God did not give me great strength... certainly for mine it is nothing!4 And now another nuisance: Fr Francesco with another priest.5 Oh! Sweetest Cross, mine, always mine!

6. Pray hard; I hope for everything from the heart of Jesus, yes; oh! Sweetest Heart! Most tender Love, oh! I want graces, and God alone can grant them. Thank you all for the prayers you say for me. Goodbye; I will finish this letter, for I must have taken it up a thousand times, what a business! Greetings to all the novices; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

What the Archbishop said is fine; she will meet the further request by sending two nurses. She declares herself glad to be poor.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. What the Archbishop said to do is fine, so I will think no more about the cook.1 Only you ask whether you should send me the travel money. Certainly one cannot travel without money, and I, a poor Franciscan, as I must always be to keep the poor Daughters of Saint Anne — and very happy I am to be so, for it is real good fortune to live as the poor.2 But if God gives me a little strength I will always spend it for Him.3

2. I do not know what to say about the stipend, for I was told they would give each of you 50 a month; isn't that so? So how does it stand now?4 Anyway, I end by asking you to pray and have others pray for me; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks her to go to Cortemaggiore to install the new Superior. The postulants will arrive; she may prepare them and hold the Clothing. Other errands.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

1. You will have received my telegram and by the time this reaches you will have done everything. Astolfi's certificate — I do not know whether you found it, for I was sure it was there.1

2. Now you need to send Sr. A. della Concezione to Cortemaggiore, for the Superior is dying; give her this letter if she is still alive; if she has died, she will read these two lines to the sisters and remain as Superior.2 Tell her something of how to proceed. If you did not feel the cold so much you could take her yourself, and then she would not even need the letters; you could do it with the two lines I enclose. You could go in the morning and come back in the evening.

3. You will see the Superior writes that she has 200 [£]; have her give it to you and send it to me at once, for there is no sign of anything that would allow me to leave.3

4. Tell the teacher not to worry, for she will have nothing to do.4

Listen, the crosses are multiplying; may God give me strength to bear it all.

5. I would need you to send me six shifts cut long; listen, did not those who were clothed have some cloth?5

Send me these shifts when I write asking you to send me sisters for Sicily.

6. If the Superior of Cortemaggiore is better, then come back and leave things as they were.

7. In a few days a fine batch of postulants will reach you;6 many have already done two or even three months; it would be good for the Parish Priest to clothe a few without telling anyone. Silence about the clothing too, or else they will go and tell; if Father Rocchi comes and has brought the fur foot-rug for the Bishop, tell him it is better to send it here to the Cardinal.7 Sr. A. Fedele will arrive, and the Superior of Toceno will come to fetch her, so try to do as I say. Dear Francesca, when shall we see each other? When I am released from house arrest.8

Goodbye; it is warm here, lovely days. Goodbye, yours for all ages affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Give £ 15 to the Parmigiani woman you know.9

She asks for news of the young teachers, one for Sestri, the other for Sicily.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you have sent the candles; it seems pointless to me; do you know why? Here we are surrounded by candles; anyway, thank you!!1

2. As for the teachers, you know one is for Sestri, and the other — which is the higher-grade one? If she cannot come, what am I to do? I would need her for Sicily;2 I assure you she would have a good Superior, Sr. A. Fabia, you know how good she is and how well they get on; besides, F. 20 a month, and I would give her something more as well.3

I await a reply. The candles have just arrived, thank you; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves what she has done and encourages her. She mentions difficulties caused by someone. Advice.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter Francesca,

1. In reply to yours: as for that wretched girl, you did well; courage, for it is time to carry a good load; what a business!!1 You will hear.

2. Now to the Superior. Next time tell her you do not have such faculties regarding Superiors, and they must apply to me;2 anyway, I hope she will recover completely and it will certainly not be needed again. Otherwise you did well.

3. As for Father Alessandro, fine, he has been up to his tricks, but how...3 This, I assure you, is a big one. How much he has done, what knots he has tied! so that I am under house arrest,4 unable to move. Arnedos, ah! now she is a famous one! She is coming here in a few days.5

4. Look in my register to see where I sent this certificate. My God, I need it desperately; I do not know what to do.

5. Sr. A. Fedele will have arrived with a postulant; well, the Superior of Toceno is coming [for] Sr. A. Fedele.6 Listen, I am writing to Lodi now about Saturnina's certificate.7 Pray for me. You must have Sr. A. Babila ready with two other sisters to send them to Bassano,8 where they are needed. Sr. A. Babila ought to learn a few easy litanies to play on the harmonium there.

Greetings to all; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She is willing to buy the house proposed by Mgr Giovannini and sets out the terms.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. In a word I reply to yours with a word.1 Tell Mgr Giovannini I am ready to buy it, provided it is over three years at ten thousand Fr. a year, and for the other 30,000 I would pay him the interest, and de mancando (?) I will try to settle sooner.2

2. Go and see whether it is suitable, so as not to regret it.3 As for the money, keep it, but for pity's sake do not spend it, understood? If I think fit I will take it;4 otherwise all is well.

Greetings to Mgr Giovannini and all the sisters; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She urges him to be prudent in dealing with the Bishop and to write to his uncle; she will explain why in person. He is to send the Arnedos power of attorney.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. First of all, if Alessandro has written to you about the Bishop of Piacenza, for pity's sake be very careful not to take any step, for it would be very wrong; do not move; for pity's sake wait, for things must be done with great prudence. Understood?1 Say nothing to Carla; let her be cheerful, for she will see many fine things mamma has done.2

2. Listen, Gaspare, I would like you to write to your uncle,3 and you must do it for me, if it is true that you love me as a mother, as I assure you I am to you. So you and Carla must write at once; do not delay a single day after this letter. I told him Carla wrote to him at Christmas. See that she says so; I thought it was true.

3. You will hear the reason in person; how much I have done for you too; in short, invite him to come.4 I really want this; you will do it at once, won't you?

4. I do not want to doubt it; I will know, for your uncle is to return. We talked of many things which I hope will please you.

5. Do not trust your brothers, still less their wives. He said nothing, nothing to me, but I learned from someone close to the family that gossip5 is always ugly — more in person; but you will hear what I have done and be pleased.

6. I would like to know whether you received a telegram from me. Ah! Prudence, I beg you; otherwise! Poor me!

Write to your uncle, and believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

7. What a slowcoach you are! If you received it, luckily I need nothing more.6 The Arnedos affair:7 we are waiting for the power of attorney; send it quickly, do not delay a moment, for I need it; otherwise I fear I shall have to stay here another year, so drawn out is it all.

I am tired; it is 10 at night; I can no longer see, though I try to keep my eyes open as long as I can!!!!

She asks her to look after a sick Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours and reply by return to say I want you to keep a very close eye on the sick sister, Sr. A. Flavia.1 A certain thought came to me.2 Watch carefully, and remember you must keep fifty eyes on the Sisters.3 I add no more, as I am in a hurry,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks them for writing to the uncle. She is sorry about the debts; she has had to spend a great deal on various matters, but will send the money as soon as possible. She longs for the hour of her return to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

Dear children,

1. Your letter was a great comfort. Ah! may God pour a thousand blessings on your heads for agreeing to my request to write to your uncle.1 He says he received no letter at Christmas; anyway, I am writing him a note today to say that your letters left Piacenza and to ask whether he has received them.

2. The reason I am staying so long in Rome is that the Rules are being approved.2

3. As for Alessandro, it was just silliness, nothing more.3

4. You tell me the butcher and the baker want to be paid. Ah! What worries! Anyway, do me the kindness of telling me how much the bills come to, and with God's help we will see to everything. See how much I have had to spend [on] the Arnedos affair. Ah! How dreadful! The Vernengo sisters, the lawyer, the rent here, the journeys of so many sisters to Sicily and to you;4 but the first [money] will be for Piacenza; write at once how much it comes to.

5. Yesterday Altieri spoke to me a lot about Carla and you. He sends his greetings; poor man, he comes with such affection!5

6. I hear Rosetta is better; look after her, she is delicate, so be careful. And Nonny, what is she doing?

7. Ah! If only I could be quick! But I have thought of doing this: I will spend 8 days in Naples and then go, I will come; they have kept me here too long, and

I [do] not yet know when I will leave, for there is much to do.6 Tell Carla I have lots of things to make her laugh.

8. I hear about the oil; I am sorry, but it will certainly arrive.

I have ordered more for the lamps.7

Goodbye. I am yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

9. Ah! If only I could see you! Patience! A big kiss to the dear little girls8

News given and asked for. She urges her to pay the debts and to get ready to leave for Rome.

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca,

1. I hope you received my letter with Carla's and Gaspare's inside; I hope all went well and no one noticed Carla's letter.

2. So the Arnedos affair1 is over; now I have the other, and today I shall hear how long they mean to keep me in agony.2

3. Listen, a postulant will have arrived; for pity's sake send the money to the one who you say is shouting in her letters.3 Oh! What a nuisance!

4. And then you should write and tell me whether you have [£] 150 to give the lawyer Galli. Write at once whether you have it, and likewise for poor Gaspare, for the [£] 550 he lent; I hear he needs it. So we must try to pay him and be done with these little debts, mustn't we?

5. Ah! If you think you are suffering, here now you would certainly see horrible things!4

Be ready, for I hope to call you soon. Meanwhile

I am thinking who should come to replace you. Yesterday, in total confusion, instead of sending you this one I sent you the lawyer's. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She speaks of the transfer of two Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Hand Sr. A. Giuliana over to the Rev. Chemin and tell her she is going to Bassano1 as portress, so she will not have to work so hard, for not many people go there. I will send Sr. A. Cornelia elsewhere. If you see you really cannot do without her,2 write to me, and believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has arranged to send her two Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hope you have already received the sister; but do not send her to that house in Spoleto; better keep her with you, so that you can send the others. Sr. A. Scolastica will also come, and you can put her in the kitchen.

2. For the rest I hope you now have enough and are content.1 Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

Lend a Sister to the Superior of Uppello for a few days.

She is surprised the Sister teacher has not been paid, while she herself has paid a lay teacher to replace her elsewhere. She is suffering and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about the stipend. I do not know what to say. Do you know what I have had to do because of Sr. A. Giuditta? Pay a fourth-class teacher for Aci Catena; I give her 27 [£]; what do you think of that?1

2. I do not understand your letter. One moment you say the cook is fine, the next not; please explain yourself better before I send the sisters.

3. So see what you can do and send me the money, for with these long journeys and changes I would need to be out begging all the time instead of sitting at my desk.2 Oh! What hellish sufferings these days!3 Pray for me, for I am in dire need! In haste,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She explains how to deal with Sisters who have shown a lack of vocation. She asks for news. Suggestions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear of Sr. A. Filippina's bad behavior; well, you will do this, which will also serve as a great example to the others. Write to her mother to be in Piacenza on Wednesday, take Sr. A. Filippina there and remove her habit. If her mother is not there, once you have removed it, tell the Superior to have Francesco take her home. Meanwhile warn her mother that we no longer want her because she is bad.1 Then we will proceed with the other one, Sr. A. Giovina Ruspigiani: tell her yourself — either good, or home.2

2. Listen, I have no sisters for nursing, and as for sending you novices among these serpents who make me lose my vocation... I certainly do not see the point.

3. I would really like to know what is wrong with Sr. A. del Crocifisso; how is she? And bring the little teacher to Piacenza, if she is well, for she is to come and fill a post with little work.

4. I hear about Sr. A. Coletta; oh! it would be a great good if she decided to leave; certainly after what she has done she must go.3 Tell her so. What trials, my God, with such heads! Try to clean house, for it is needed. Before she goes, have her sign a paper stating she has no claim on the Institute. If she mentions the old rags she brought, you can tell her they will kindly be accepted against what she should have given and did not; and more would certainly be owed to us.4

5. But let them go, for they are truly the ones who hold back divine Providence; once they are gone I will send you two good ones, but first these must go. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to send the Sisters, prepare the postulants' clothing, and leave with Sr. A. Michelina Negri.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This morning when writing I forgot to tell you that with those you are to send me you must include the Devoto girl who is at Lodi; send her with the lay woman, with Sr. A. Pompilia and the ones I mentioned.1

2. Listen, as soon as Sr. A. Consolata2 arrives, come at once; meanwhile clothe the Postulants as best you can; make their habits at once, so that at least by Monday they are clothed.3

3. You should be here on Wednesday at 6 a.m., for on Thursday, God willing, we are going to dinner at the Parrocchietta, and you will come too. I am expecting you; be sure to bring a new habit, and Sr. A. Michelina too, for you will go to the audience; the veil must be spotless and new.4 So leave on Tuesday at one o'clock and, traveling straight through, you will be here the next day!

4. I commend Sr. A. Michelina to you — for pity's sake at night, you know? Be careful.5

5. Let me know how many novices there are, including those you will clothe, and the postulants. One will arrive from Recanati; leave word about her. Goodbye; I am tired; it is late

your affectionate M. ROSA

She expresses deep gratitude and thank-, fulness for his kindness and protection towards the FSA of the Nurses' House and the Institute.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I have no words adequate to express my gratitude for the good you do the poor Daughters of Saint Anne of the Nurses' House.1

2. I assure you, Excellency, that I shall always remember the fatherly care you show us; and the Lord will reward Your Excellency with His most abundant blessings, for the kindnesses and attentions you show the poor Daughters of Saint Anne are countless.

3. So, Excellency, please accept these words of thanks as a token of my everlasting gratitude, trusting always that Your Excellency will continue your kindness and protection towards our poor Institute.

4. Prostrate at your feet I ask your Pastoral Blessing, and kissing your sacred ring with deepest respect I remain

Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most devoted Servant Sister Anna ROSA GATTORNO

She asks her to bring two teachers to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I would like you to do me a favor: having brought me the higher-grade teacher, whom I accept at £ 27 as you say,1 go or send to Sestri for the sister teacher and bring her to me in Piacenza with the lay woman.

2. Then at Sestri put the lay teacher you say you have found.2 That is how I wish and want it. For the rest, pray and have others pray! I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to pay the lawyer and ask Sr. A. Consolata to look after the postulants well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I enclose £ 700: 500 for the lawyer and another 150 for him as well; that leaves you £ 50. Send for him at once, for payment falls due on the 22nd. You see there is no time to lose.1

2. Meanwhile, for pity's sake, when you leave on Tuesday, commend the postulants warmly to Sr. A. Consolata, for I am very anxious.2 Listen, one is to come from Ventimiglia, a teacher who is to be clothed as a Daughter of Saint Anne, but not now, on your return; tell Sr. A. Consolata to keep her with her and keep her cheerful, for pity's sake. I would not want her to be put off; I commend her to you, for pity's sake.

I await you with open arms,

affectionate M. ROSA

She approves, asks for news and answers a request.

A.M.F.

My daughter for ever,

1. Very well done; always behave like this with the Confessor and with everyone.1 As for the house, are you not telling me any more about it?2

2. For that Sister's papers you will have to go back to Piacenza, for I have nothing here.3

Greetings to the Sisters, especially Sr. A. Eletta, and believe me yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

She gives the permission asked and encourages her in her educational work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in reply, to grant your wish.1 You tell me about the girls.2 Ah! yes, my daughter, I will pray that God gives you strength to do everything well3 and gives the girls supernatural understanding.4 Keep your spirits up, for the Saint will do it; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks to be told when he has written to his uncle. She commends Carla to him and advises him not to visit the Sisters. He is to keep the door shut and send her the plan of the house drawn as she explained.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. Last night I received another letter from you, and I hope you received mine today, telling you both to write at once to your uncle with many, many compliments. For pity's sake do it at once and write as soon as you have sent it, so that I can go to the office myself and find out; then he will have no more excuses.1

2. I strongly commend Carla to you; she must not fret, for as the time approaches when she brought up blood, it could certainly return. I am anxious; I commend her to you warmly; let her be cheerful.

3. Listen, you should now take care not to go to the nuns at all unless absolutely necessary. Do as I say and you will be glad of it; do not get involved in anything, keep the door shut, and send me what I asked for: the plan drawn as I told you.2

4. Please look into the oil.3 Goodbye, for I am going to the Vatican.

5. Ah! how the Holy Father has comforted me! Ah! how he received me! You will hear. Ah! sweet Father!

Many kisses to the little dolls and a thousand affectionate wishes to you both; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks her and asks for prayers and the Archbishop's blessing. She cannot come to Palermo, having much to do. The Sisters will arrive.1

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. Thank you for the lovely expressions of affection you show me, unworthy as I am;2 tell the sisters their words were welcome amid so many troubles. Pray hard for me, for this is a time when I truly need it. Thank the Archbishop and ask him for a big blessing for me; I fear I cannot come this year, for I still have much to do.3

2. Another house is opening here,4 so there is work to be done; only I have no strength, for I see I am growing old and full of sins, and my back is bending. Goodbye, yours; with greetings to all the sisters I am for all ages your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Two sisters will arrive with the lay teacher; send Sr. A. Annunciata and the lay teacher straight on to Aci Catena; Sr. A. Antonina is for Sr. A. Salvatore's nurses' house. Goodbye; I would like you to show the little teacher a thousand kindnesses and keep her happy, for then she will become a sister; I very much hope so, for she is so good.5

She will arrange for the Sister to be sent what she asks for.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line, for it is late and I am very tired. I commend the sister to you; tell her to send me separately a little list of what she lacks, and I will have it sent to her at once by writing there; she need not doubt it.1

2. Let her be at peace; I commend her to you; watch her closely and do not trust her.2

Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

She has received the registered letter. Thanks and greetings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your registered letter; thank you for everything;1 I wrote yesterday and now limit myself2 to telling you that the days pass quickly and, God willing, we shall see each other. I am delighted to hear you like the cook.

Many greetings to the sisters, and to you a thousand affectionate wishes in the Sacred Heart of Jesus, where I hold you close; I am affectionate M. ROSA

She has heard of their worry about the children's cough epidemic in Piacenza and urges care to avoid infection. She is also very anxious about Carlotta. She has accepted a crèche and hopes to return soon.1

A.M.F.

Dear Gaspare and Carla,
