1. Cheer up, for everything is over and nothing more is needed; just a little more patience to finish, then I will leave everything and come back. I will stay in Naples only 8, at most 10 days, and then fly to you; God willing we shall see each other soon.

2. You say you fear the cough; for pity's sake keep them away from the girls so they see none of them, for it is horribly catching; you know we escaped the German measles and they had nothing, but protect them, for pity's sake. Otherwise the only thing would be a change of air, but God forbid. Here it is worse; there are a thousand diseases, if you only heard.2

3. I hear about Carla and am very anxious, for the fatal time of the bleeding is approaching; for pity's sake, cheerfulness!3 Yes, my Carla, listen, in a few days the Superior will return and then I will come straight away, for I assure you I would like to fly.

4. I have good news for you: listen, I have accepted a crèche.4 Ah! what a lovely place, fitted out with every elegance! If Carla saw it she would fall in love with it. 32 cradles, all elegantly fitted; you will hear in person; it means a great deal of work for me, for I must do everything. We are in a good haven: it is right in the tobacco factory, and we deal with no one but the Commendatore, a young and very distinguished man.5

5. Imagine, I have had all the layettes made in the big shop in Via del Corso, the finest; imagine, they are all to be dressed in white; the cradles are all curtained with white muslin. Ah! it is lovely; I will tell you how they are washed; this kind and charitable gentleman comes often to see how things are going. It is a comical scene; you will hear what laughing you must not do!! Tomorrow I am going to order their nappies and swaddling bands; everything is already in order.6

6. I said nothing; this evening your uncle7 came, beside himself over the letters he had received; now, when you receive his reply, write to him and tell him to hand over your interests to me, likewise your share of your grandmother's (inheritance), which the others have already received.

7. Read it as best you can; it is late, I am tired, and early tomorrow I must go out to buy things for the babies.

Ah! dear Nonny and Nonetto, if you saw how many babies! how funny! you would take them all in your arms and rock them to sleep. How funny!8 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She does not think the Sister suggested is suitable. She is unwell and has an immense amount of work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in reply. Well done, daughter!1 As for granting you the sister you ask for, I tell you she is not capable; if you want Sr. A. Ulderica, yes, she is capable, but I fear they need her.2 I would like to tell you many things, but I have a headache and an immense amount of work,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Greetings to all

She has heard that Rosetto has a cough and suggests remedies. News of her work and travels. She sends money to repay an expense and awaits news.

A.M.F.

My dearest son,

1. How has it all come upon everyone at once? Is it really true that Rosetto has whooping cough?1 My God! I have no more peace; write to Signora Maddalena, and send a nun at once to fetch the decoction,2 and try to separate Nonny.3 Ah! It is so nasty.

2. Poor little thing, give her a change of air at once! If you want to come here, do, but there is smallpox in Rome and diphtheria,4 so I do not know what to tell you; it has given me such a shaking that I do not know what to do; I cannot move; if you think Carla would like to come, bring her.

3. Tomorrow is my last meeting with His Eminence and others on the points of the Rules,5 and on Monday the 14th the crèche opens;6 on Tuesday, God willing, I leave for Naples, where I will stay barely 10 days, no more, and then fly to Piacenza. What am I to do? And then there is my health, and you know how little I have.

4. So call the doctor. Orange-flower water irritates the bronchial tubes. Be very careful! She must have caught cold, and that brought on the cough. And Carla, what is she getting into her head?

5. At last only a few days are left and then I will be there. Be cheerful, for I will bring you lots of lovely things; but if Carla is ill I will bring her nothing and go off to Sicily.7 I want to hear she is cheerful and content, understood?

6. I hear about Tinelli. There is nothing in it; tell him I have written that there is nothing in it and that I do not intend to pay the coachman for the Marchioness; I think it must have been for her.8 I am sending you the [£] 500 you gave the lawyer, and later I will send the money for the bread, as you say.9 You can tell him I have written that I will send it; if I can I will add [£] 100, which you will send him; the rest I will pay when I arrive. I hope the Lord will send it to me.

7. Goodbye. I am extremely anxious. Carla, write at once and tell me what is wrong; [and] you, Nonny me,10 for pity's sake keep well, for I am coming soon. Goodbye

your affectionate M. ROSA

She will see to the house. Let her ensure the girls are treated well by their teachers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about the house. Tomorrow I will speak to the Cardinal about it and then write to Mgr Giovannini.1

2. It grieves me to hear from your second letter of the bad temper and lack of charity towards the little girls;2 it pains me greatly, but you must keep watch over everything; enough. I am now writing kindly about it to Sr. A. Eletta;3 for the rest, patience! Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letter and written to one Sister. She should do her best about another.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your long account. Ah! Sadly that soul will need it. Ah! If only it had served as an example to certain others. Ah! What a conversion they ought to make, oughtn't they?1 Yesterday I wrote to you enclosing one for Sr. A. Coletta.2 My God, convert them!

2. I had you told that if Sr. A. del Crocifisso keeps getting worse, you should take her to Invorio in the hope that she would be quiet for a few months. So I leave you to do what is best.3

3. I would like to know whether that rich lady left you anything.4

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters, and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

She encloses the receipt for a basket sent. She is preparing to leave for Naples. She tells Carla to be cheerful and pray. She asks for news.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. I enclose the receipt for a basket containing vegetables, tomatoes and a few grapes for the two little ones, who can eat them without harm; the vegetables are for you two.

2. Today the meeting went well! And everything is over.1 I am overwhelmed with packing for departure.2

3. Carla, be cheerful and come to meet me. Write to me, for I am anxious. Here they use curious saddlebag-shaped muffs, but winter is over and it seems pointless.3

4. Please make the month of St Joseph and, if you want graces, pray to dear Most Holy Mary; we must obtain everything from her; that is how everything is obtained.4

Goodbye; I am anxious for news of dear Rosette and my dear Nonny! Dear! Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She invites her to come, as she wants to talk to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear that plague of relatives is still tormenting you;1 so come straight into my arms, for you know they have been your cradle for many years and want only your good.2

2. So come, and before you go to your post3 I can talk to you. Meanwhile be strong and listen to no one but the one who is ever your affectionate M. ROSA

Sorry to hear of her poor health, she urges her to look after herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in reply: how is it that you have a fever? For pity's sake take care! And yet there are no fevers in that city.1 Do not overtax yourself; try to get well.

2. I hear about the others, but I think it will be something minor.2 I am still in Rome with a great deal to do, but I hope to be ready by Monday and able to leave, God willing.3 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She tells her she has written to Mgr Giovannini about buying the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line; listen, you certainly did not do well about the girl and the confessor, for that is always giving them a foothold; enough.1

2. I have written to Mgr Giovannini telling him I cannot spend more than sixty to sixty-five, with twenty thousand at once and the rest in instalments.2

Goodbye; I am busy,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has already written and hopes the Sister will soon have everything.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours with the note; all is well; I sent it on at once and hope Sr. A. Speciosa will have everything within 10 days.1 So cheer up, for over so little it is not worth leaving Jesus, who is our all.2 Ah! what a devil, he is truly raging against Jesus' spouses!

Goodbye; greetings to Speciosa; in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

Instructions about two girls.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours and hear you repeat that you did it as a joke, regarding the Confessor.1 It seems to me badly done,2 and I would not want it to happen again.

1. Now I must tell you that Verginietta,3 this August, when she has finished her examinations, will come to Rome to be confirmed, for she wants to be her sponsor.4 So be careful not to have her confirmed there. Understood? When there is an opportunity for nuns to come here, she will travel with them, at that time, I mean. The nuns are all four for me.5 I hope they have already left. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is worried about her sick granddaughter. Advice about Carla's health.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. I hear what you say about Rosette; how sad!!! I assure you it is a martyrdom to see that I cannot move and then hear such things about the little girls!

2. Listen, I am sure poor Rosette has had what happened to me when I caught bronchitis again at Pistoia, worse than the first time. So you should put a Milan fly on her chest,1 which will do her a lot of good, and then milk, always milk. A cough is a nasty enemy.

3. I hear about Carla; it is better this way than an illness,2 but see that she does not ride in a carriage, for the danger point is terrible, as last time.3 Once that time is past she can do as she likes, but now she must not overdo it, for pity's sake. She should stay in bed or sitting, not get angry or worried; I beg you.

4. God willing, on Tuesday I shall be in Naples, where I will stay only 8 or 10 days, and then I will come. Cheer up, for now everything is over. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

Encouragement and exhortation.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line, though I really have not a moment to breathe. Listen, you tell me you work for Jesus — and are you not happy?1 Ah! we must all walk for Jesus; blessed are you if you do so. Think of being observant2 and believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

Advice for Carla. She is worried about her granddaughter's health.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. I understood perfectly what you told me about Carla's condition, and you will see from my previous letter, which you will now have, that I understood; that is why I repeat: tranquillity, peace, and not too much riding in carriages.1

3. I fear you are not looking after her properly, that the woman lets her catch cold. Oh! a thousand things! They will give her too much of this medicine, and who knows about that one; it worries me greatly. I want to hear she is well, and soon; so look after her!4

4. Tell Carla I have made the acquaintance of a very rich Commendatore who will come to Piacenza; you will see how good he is.5 We often talk about you two and the dear little ones. Nonny me,6 tell me, what shall I bring you?

your affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

1. Well done; that is the way.1 When someone has nothing but love for her own house and wants to make the honor of her own Institute shine, she acts as you have done.2

your affectionate M. ROSA

My son,

2. My daughter,

1. You want my handwriting, my God!1 Pray for me, that God may give me strength to do everything. It is late at night and I assure you I can do no more; I feel truly tired and can hardly stand up straight for weariness.2 Do whatever you think right in holy observance, and believe me

Most Reverend Excellency,

My daughter,

She is to send off a Sister and novices.1

My daughter,

1. A line to repeat, with great displeasure I repeat, that you are to send what you have2 together with Sr. A. Cunegonda and two novices. After all, I find people come and go easily, and when one wants to, everything gets done.3 Goodbye,

your affectionate M.5 ROSA

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta,

1. Send me a cutlet for Nonny, who by God's mercy is hungry and wants you to send a cutlet; send me the shawls and something to cover myself with.2

She has reached Fiorenzuola and the lovely little house Don Piacenza has prepared. Nonny is well and no longer coughing.

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta,

1. We arrived safely; dear Don Piacenza was at the station with a carriage. I cannot tell you what this Angel does and has prepared, my God! How grateful I feel!1

2. If you knew what a lovely little house, with its own oratory, the Lord has given us! Today I arranged the furniture; it really is a beautiful house. Oh! when Carla can come, how happy she will be!

3. Magnificent air; Nonny has not coughed again and eats like a dragon; we have ordered a little goat;2 she is truly happy. At least we shall save one. Oh! If only they had done this — you know how often I told them. I cannot think of it without feeling choked. I hope she is alive!3

4. Enough; do not forget to send me the paper. Don Piacenza's sister came too. What a dear person; they do a thousand things for us; I am quite overwhelmed. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She thinks of her children with great anguish. Nonny is better. The days seem like centuries.1

A.M.F.

Dear Benedetta,

1. In haste, for the post is leaving. How are they? How must my Carla be? I am constantly plunged in a deathly agitation; how I suffer! To think of Carla and Gaspare — though I think he is a hero; I am certainly nothing like him in this.2 I am a fool, for all my resignation.3 Oh! days full of true sorrow!

2. Nonny is a little better; her blocked nose has cleared, the cough is slight, and everyone tells me that in three or four days we shall see a good improvement.

3. I assure you that, what with this place and everything, far from you all and from poor Carla, the days seem like centuries. I hope to write again this evening. Greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

I enclose these two letters; if you think fit, give them to Gaspare.

She hopes they will meet again. She has suffered and still suffers greatly from the loss of her granddaughter.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have your letter. I hear three novices have eye trouble; yes, send them at once to the Morte.1 As for Sr. A. Irene, tell her I am expecting her here with me, so that when you come you can bring her.2

2. I hope the quarantine will soon be over,3 so that you can come here and I can come there, which I so need.

3. For two days I have felt utterly worn out; perhaps you think that, being with Nonny, I need not feel what has happened;4 on the contrary, I can say it for myself: alone and so seized by grief, without anyone to say a word to... Oh! Enough; I hope I have drunk the chalice of bitterness and sorrow to the last drop.

4. Oh! what sorrow! Enough; Jesus wills it so, and may his divine will be done; in haste I am [...] tell Sr. A. Benedetta I have received her letter and had already written to her. Ah! I can hardly wait to see you!

Your affectionate M. ROSA

Nonny is better. She should go with Carla to Milan to take her mind off things and comfort her. Grief still prevents the Mother from writing to her. They can meet on Sunday, four days from now.1

A.M.F.

Dearest and more than dearest daughter,

1. I take the chance to write you a couple of lines today too; we can breathe a little; Nonny is somewhat better, for she certainly had a lot,2 enough. With great care I found an excellent children's doctor, who prescribed a little syrup that did her so much good. Today she coughed only twice, and slightly, even though the weather is dreadful.

2. As for going to Milan with Carla,3 the expense is small, so you can do it, poor thing. One day she will see how much her mamma loves her. Had I not done this, my God! enough; I cannot tell you what this poor child has suffered and still suffers!

3. Alone, I must always drive away as an evil temptation the mere thought "she is no more", my God!4 I think I feel it as much as her mother and father.

4. Dear Benedetta, if you think it will help poor Carla, take her to Milan; the expense is small and I will bear it; it is a work of charity; let it be done; God helps. My dear Benedetta, get the money from the Superior;5 for the rest, do as you see fit.

5. Tell Carla of the sacrifice I am making for her dear daughter, who, God willing, is recovering; I hope she will think of how hard her mamma is working for her. I am not writing to her, for I still cannot bring my pen to write to them both.

6. If you go to Milan, enjoy yourselves; she must not overdo it; let her often remember her condition, for soon she will have another baby to comfort her.

7. What did the doctor say about when you can come? They say that to be safe we must let at least 8 days pass, and then it is safer. So we cannot meet until Saturday or Sunday. Carla must be longing to see her, but it will not be wise to meet [until] Saturday evening or better Sunday morning. I keep counting the days: tomorrow Wednesday, so four more. They seem to me years and centuries that never pass.

8. I urge Sr. A. Francesca to take care of herself, to spare nothing and get treatment.6 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

And you do the same; look after yourself, for pity's sake. Greetings to Carla and Gaspare.

My daughter,

As for the sister, let her go home, but out of her religious habit; you will keep her habits, and she will put them on again when she returns; that is all.2 You will say: "And her dress, Mother?3 You could lend her one; otherwise I will send one, but it will take too long; I am at Fiorenzuola and up to my neck in business.4 I am your affectionate M. My daughter,

My daughter,

My daughter,

1. I hear how troubled you are about the sisters;1 your own fault; I always say: "whoever obeys blindly never fails". If instead of Fr Rocchi a Sister had come with a novice — if you did not know whom to send you could have sent Sr. A. Cunegonda to accompany them, and she would then have returned — how good that would have been!2

2. For then I could have spoken to her in person, things would have been arranged much better, and a nun would have been removed from there who, in my view, spoils them all and takes away the peace — Sr. A. Clelia!3 She ought to be taken out of that hospital, for as long as she stays there you will have no peace.

3. I always keep the fine maxim of keeping the threshing floor clean; if out of self-interest you keep what is rotten, it will end by depriving you of providence. That is false economy.4

So do your sums and see whether you can send her, kindly, without telling her anything. Then, when she is here, I will take her habit from her; but you must not tell her.

You must be pleasant to her and treat her kindly; meanwhile you could send me everything you have, not by her, for that would be making us public, but by whoever accompanies her.6 Enough; that would be my idea, but if you see it is not right, or that something else would work better, then leave it. 6. I have received the accounts and the two letters together, Sr. A. Cunegonda's; yesterday another came enclosing one from Sr. A. Zoe. The accounts are in order.

My daughter,

6. Goodbye! Greetings to all, and I send them a thousand blessings. Let them all hear these words of mine, and tell them I await letters from them to relieve my anguish. My God, what grief!

1. A line in reply. The sisters arrived safely; I saw and greeted them. As for the things, you will take them yourself when you come this August, as you know.

3. I would like you to tell Mgr Ricci himself that all the alms she has sent to the Holy Father were always at our Father's prompting.2 If he does not come, write to him what I tell you: that she will soon send it,3 for she asked for the address, and I hope he will receive it. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves her efforts and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just one line; I am weighed down with work. You did everything well for Mgr Ricci. The Marchioness is now in Milan, but as soon as she returns the Father will do all he can to obtain what is desired.1 For the rest — oh, dear daughter, far from austerity for me, quite the opposite! You know [I am] a sinner and that Jesus has punished me for the treats I indulged in. Pray for me and believe me; I would like to tell you so many things, but I can do no more,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to send off the Sister, who must be sent back to her family.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter; you will have received mine; send me Sr. A. Coletta, and then there will be nothing more to say.1 I hear about the one who left. Oh! what a business!2 I have received everything; I am not very well and am overwhelmed with work. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letter. The Marchioness is not yet back; she will let her know.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was most dear to me. God bless you, and may he be blessed [and] thanked throughout the world. Dear Jesus, may everything be done for you alone!

2. Yes, our holy Mother always helps her daughters in a special way. The Marchioness is not yet back; she sent word she will return on Monday, and then the Father will learn something at once and I will write to you.1 Now I must stop, for, as you know, I am [so busy], and I remain ever your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received two letters with distressing news. She is preparing four Sisters; sending six is impossible because of the cost. Any sacrifice must be made to send back to Italy those who dishonor the Institute.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply at once to your two letters, which I have just received together, one dated 13 March and the other 6 April; I do not know why there are these delays.1

2. For the rest I hear with the greatest sorrow the bad news of the sisters; what grief! This truly pierces my soul, to think that instead of edifying they went there to pierce the heart of Jesus. Oh! senseless little creatures! To betray their Spouse in that way? What are they doing?2

3. Here the sisters study very well and are very capable; I hope you will be pleased. You tell me to send six. Oh! yes, I would gladly do so, but how am I to pay for the journey? And now I have no means! [and] so many people! I had to build the new Chapel and add a wing to the house for the Novitiate. You see? Everything must come out of these bones; I have no income.

4. The pharmacists are studying, and Spanish too; the pianist is excellent, and in everything else as well.3

5. As for the other matters, it would be well to make any sacrifice in time rather than wait for scandals to arise from the Sisters' divisions; that would be very painful, and they would all come to a very bad end.4

6. This I tell them and repeat: whoever betrays Jesus cannot end well. Oh! how differently these in Italy behave, conducting themselves so well. Young girls full of zeal and love for their Institute — while those who ought to give good counsel and be true champions of the Institute!

7. Sacrifice anything; send here those wretches who can do nothing but feed their self-love, vipers of the Institute who devour it with their poison.

8. As for the pharmacist, you will see that [they are] two angels and well trained; but surely, if the bad ones are not removed before they arrive, what will happen? They will infect them. Oh! where is the holiness of our Sisters? I am in the greatest anguish.5

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She is authorized to buy the house and specifies the price, terms and date of the contract.

[Reverend Monsignor,]

1. Only at this moment has the reply of His Eminence the Protector reached me,1 gladly agreeing to the purchase of the house in Florence and leaving me full authority to negotiate it according to the Institute's means.2

2. So stop at fifty thousand lire, and if the seller agrees to that sum, fix the contract for the end of next June on the terms Your Excellency proposed: thirty thousand lire on purchase, and twenty thousand to be paid with interest. That is what the Institute can take on, and no more.3

3. Please accept my sincere thanks for all the trouble you take for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne.

With deep esteem I remain

your humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She has received her letters. The postulant seems good.

Dear daughter,

1. I have received your letters; they were most dear to me. Well done, daughter; be at peace, and let us hope that in August we shall be together more.

2. The young woman seems good to me.1

I would like to tell you so many things, but you know how I am placed. So I am yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

She cannot come for the moment; she may perhaps stop on her way through Legnano.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

My immense workload does not allow me to move, but perhaps, as I have to pass through Legnano, I will try to stop.1 As for the trip to Our Lady, I think you should first try to get completely well.2 Meanwhile we shall see each other first, and everything will be better arranged in person.

I urge economy and observance; in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She approves what she has done and asks for news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was a real comfort; keep sending me reports.1 You did well to have those children clothed. But you tell me nothing about your health, or whether you are happy there, yes or no.2 For the rest, take heart and believe me ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

She allows her to go to Lugo for confession.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste; show these two lines to the Superior. Sr. A. Agnese is permitted to confess to the Lugo Confessor.1

2. I am not replying to both of you, as I am in the greatest haste. I do not allow outings, only this one to Lugo, and only out of sheer necessity. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to go to Genoa to collect the inheritance. Advice on the matter.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. The lawyer1 has just come to tell me the bonds have arrived in Genoa;2 so leave at once, and if you see they want to raise objections or deceive you, telegraph, and I will send the lawyer at once.

2. If Accinelli tells you something must be paid, tell him to apply to the lawyer Galli and he will be paid at once; he need not doubt: if we settled the other accounts, these will be settled too, have no doubt.

3. Go at once, so that I can use them. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Come here; I will expect you once you have collected everything. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks for a medical certificate. The alms-collecting is to be suspended.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line, as I am in haste. I would like your doctor to certify that she needs her native air; then send her to her mistress, who told me she would send for her.1

2. For now, do not send out the alms-collectors.2 I will tell you the reason in person. Wholly your affectionate M. ROSA

She writes in her own hand to reassure her. Five Sisters are to sit their examinations. Other news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to please you; but how can I write to everyone? My God! Why do you behave like this? You are not content when I have letters written for me. Ah! what a pity; if you knew how it grieves me, you would surely sympathize. Enough!

2. Listen, I would like you to be at ease about that Fr. — You never write me anything! I can assure you I am now corresponding with him, for I have five nuns to send for their diploma and I know he has much influence, does he not?1

3. For the rest, be cheerful. The Province has not yet sent me anything; as soon as it does, I will send it on to you.2 About the teachers I cannot yet tell you anything.3 Let us hope these two you have there do not make up their minds!

4. Rest assured I am fully aware of your affection and do not doubt it; I have had proof enough.

Goodbye; yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

Summons to the Mother House for the spiritual exercises, with instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. We inform you that you must be at the Mother House in Piacenza on 15 August.1

2. Therefore: 1st, set aside the money for your journey there and back; 2nd, leave in your place for the few days of absence the sister you judge most suitable before God; 3rd, try to arrange with the Superiors nearest you to travel together; 4th, bring the half-yearly accounts for 1881.

May the Lord bless the whole Community.

Gio. BATT. TORNATORE Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

My daughter,2

The circular will tell you what to do, so I add nothing more, for, God willing, we shall see each other.

Your affectionate M. R.

She entrusts this letter to the alms-collectors. She could not hand over the Province's money because she has not yet received it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. By way of your alms-collectors, who came to see me — I was very pleased, for they gave me so much good news from there. Thanks be to God, and a thousand blessings to you.

2. I would have liked to give them the Province's money, but I had not yet managed to get it. What people! What a fuss they make about paying!1

3. I am sending you the circular.2 I will tell you many things in person; I am so busy and so sunk in troubles. Dear daughter, courage, all for Jesus!

I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks her and answers a question.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line: thank you for the altar cloth, it is very beautiful.1 I am delighted to hear your health is better; blessed be God for healing you. I am writing to the Rector this very day.2

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She is in favor of letting a sick Sister go to her family; once recovered she will be taken back.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I hope the sisters have called and collected the postulant.1 It would be good for the sister to try a little of her native air,2 and I gladly grant it; indeed, have her accompanied; and I promise her that as soon as she recovers she will be taken back into the house. Write to me, for you can accompany her. I will send you the money for the journey.

2. As you will see from the circular, in August I shall be able to embrace you and tell you many things in person. I am your affectionate M. ROSA

Advice and news.

A.M.F.

Dear Santina,

1. Accept the postulants you mention; make sure they have a trousseau and certificates and are good and strong.

2. I hear about the Donati lady;1 do all you can, help as much as possible; do not abandon her.

3. I could not reply by telegram to Mgr Giovannini, as I was away.2 Greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

The Marchioness is back and the Father is trying to persuade her. Instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste, for I know well you need my own handwriting, or else!1 So the Father keeps pressing the Marchioness on behalf of the Holy Father; she arrived from Milan the day before yesterday and told him she will send it soon.2

2. For the rest, you will soon receive the circular, which will tell you the day you are to come; it will serve as your guide.3 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

You must not now give any more money to Margana,4 for you will need it for the journey there and back. Goodbye, your [affectionate M. R.]

She has written to Mgr Giovannini about the contract to buy the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have written to Mgr Giovannini that if you are ready to pay the amount above the fifty thousand — which I believe will be only a thousand, won't it? — then you may go ahead.1 I have told him to close the contract.

2. The letters were delayed because I was away. Please keep an eye on Sr. A. Dionigia2 (for the rest). I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She urges her to look after herself and asks her to pass on to the two Superiors what she writes about them.1

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your dearest letter and hear that Gherzi2 found what I had said; it was all too clear. What a pity! Oh! dear daughter, if only you were a little more open with one who loves you surely more than a mother! So see that you never do that again.3

2. Today we are celebrating here, as you surely are there too.4

3. Tell the Superior to keep strong and well, so that you will come here sturdy.5 I have written to the Sestri Superior and told her that if she has anything to say, she should say it to you.6 She wanted to come here, but it is really pointless, for the days fly by and on 15 August I shall see her with the others.7

4. I am so overwhelmed that writing is an effort. You know how much I have to do!

Dear Francesca, believe me for all ages

your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Warm greetings to your mamma and papa and sisters; you are mine for eternity...

She warns her that she may not accumulate money to buy the house and advises her to bring the sum herself. She urges vigilance and the avoidance of abuses.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply to your two letters; I have also received those of the Sisters, which I will answer at once, and more fully still, one by one, when the sisters who are studying come out to you; I assure you they are very good.1

2. Now let us talk a little about money. I hear with great surprise that you are accumulating a sum to buy a house there;2 that is certainly not according to the Lord's will. If benefactors gave you such a sum, whatever you came [to] have you must send to Italy, you understand?3

3. I think you could come yourself; then you would return with these sisters and see how they have been prepared; moreover we could better see how other contracts should be made.4 Sr. A. Cunegonda could take your place for four months, and you could come with the bad ones.5

4. Oh! listen, I repeat what I have written so often: it is better to have less money than for the Institute to suffer harm and lose everything for the sake of two thousand.6

I repeat: had it been done like that — oh! poor Institute!

5. We must be less attached when it is a question of the Institute. Oh! how it grieves me to think that so many things happen there that do the Institute no honor. Oh! the first ones, from whom I expected something very different.7

6. So be careful, and look at your lack of vigilance: letting the sisters go out to lunch at the Bishop's niece's — oh! how dreadful!8

7. My dear, what! You know it all; surely, losing the spirit little by little, what happens? The devil gets to work and many ugly things happen; such as being too much in contact with the apprentices, leaving a man in the dispensary.9 Oh! what lack of judgment! Let me tell you so.

8. Be patient, but you know that on this point I am more jealous than I can say. For pity's sake reassure me and come, it is better so, for many reasons; obey.

[your affectionate M. ROSA]

She thanks her for her letter and urges her to keep well and not overtire herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was most dear to me. Thank you for the wax.1 But listen, it is not worth your buying it. Hearing you have none, I have approached another place that has some, so I will have it sent; you will send me something else. Meanwhile, ah! yes, I long to see you, all the more since it concerns...2 Enough, dear daughter; keep well and do not overtire yourself, for pity's sake, that is all we need.3

2. If God is pleased to grant me life, I hope it will be done well with your help. So do not wear yourself out, you understand? Always think of the one who holds you in the Heart of Jesus and remains your affectionate M. ROSA

Instructions for the summer period.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. What did you say to Signor Simonetta?1 Tell him I am happy to leave you there, and that if you have to leave, as was always done in other years, you will; otherwise I do not know what to write to him.

2. You will tell me this in person; we shall see each other by 15 August and then sort it all out better face to face, if God grants me life. I am your affectionate M. ROSA

1. I have received the accounts and the letters;2 tell the sisters to renew their Vows; I allow it to all of them, to you, and to the novice too.

2. For the rest, we shall see each other.3 I cannot allow the sisters to come for 15 August, as there is no room at that time.4 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is very worried that her illness persists. She sends two Sisters, one for the Genoa house and the other to prepare for examinations.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear from Sr. A. Benedetta2 that you still have some stomach pain. My God! does it never go? Tell me exactly how it is, for I am more anxious than you can believe.3 I wish you were here; if your letters do not come every day I feel restless. For pity's sake, dear Francesca, take care of yourself and get well quickly.

2. Tell mamma I am not writing to her because I am so overwhelmed with work that I do not know how to get everything done.

3. Listen, I am sending you Sr. A. Eustochia; put her in that house as wardrobe-keeper and tell the Superior to keep a close eye on her, never let her go out, and not let her make friends with the Sisters.4 Let them beware of her, for she is flighty. I think that if this is done we can be fairly easy; she must not be able to write, for she is too crafty and will do anything to send letters.5 In short, watch her closely. I say no more.

4. This is another one6 for the examinations; she is so good; her only fault is being very shy. Encourage her; I will send yet another. Yours for ever, affectionate M. ROSA

She approves what she has done and advises her on certain situations in the two communities.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This morning I sent you a letter by the Sisters, and now I receive two from you.2 All you have done is right; well done! You had better call the two at S.P. d'Arena to Genoa at once, at once, for it is not right for them to stay there. The reason is strong enough to remove them.3

2. For the rest, regarding Sestri, do as you say; write and do the accounts as you say.4

3. For pity's sake take care of yourself and try to be well for Saint Anne's day, as soon as you go to the baths.5 Sr. A. Michelina is so well that she says she can do without them, so I am not sending her. Look after yourself, look after yourself, spare nothing; believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

4. Tell the Superior she has done everything well, that I thank her for all of it and wish her a thousand blessings;6 I am not writing to her, as I am overwhelmed with work; I am yours...

5. Listen, Sr. A. Gemma Gandino writes that she wants to go to America. See whether she is really good and would be capable of training and studying as a pharmacist; if she writes her own letters she is very able; tell me something.7

She speaks to her of her daughter's health and character. She may also invite her to lunch or dinner; she gladly permits it. She wishes her to recover completely.

A.M.F.

Dear Elisa,

1. I hear what you tell me about dear Sr. A. Francesca; believe me, [her illness] was caused neither by overwork nor by lack of care, for God alone could tell you how much I strove, but it is precisely her taciturn nature, in which one has to guess whether she feels unwell,1 I assure you that many times I was greatly distressed,2 and I always tormented her by telling her it is not good to keep silent, and that is why I resolved to send her.3

2. As for the work, there is nothing to be done. I am only concerned for her health, as I have always told her; so I leave you in full charge to have her treated to the point of scruple, to follow the doctor's orders, and so, when she wishes to come, whether to lunch or to dinner, let her come, for I am most content.4

3. You will then know her timid nature better than I do; so [you will see to it] that she is not disturbed. I always think it best not to disturb her, to leave her very much in peace, because angels love to stay hidden, and I know she suffers greatly if she has to leave her habits; I have never upset her.5

4. You, as a mother, will know better than I. Of Mamma, nothing new. I close, greeting everyone and asking you to tell me of yourself; always yours

affectionate Sister Rosa

Today, by good fortune, I have a headache; be patient!

She insists that she take proper care of herself. Advice about two Sisters.1

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca,

1. Listen, first of all you must promise me to look after yourself without stinting, either time or anything else, so long as you are here on the eve of the Saint's feast; that is enough. Your health comes first.

2. So your mother wants you to come to lunch; please them; you know what lay people are like.2 Ah! the illness: great patience.

3. I hear what you say about the sister. Oh! If you can, send me the note.3 Listen, keep a close eye on Sr. A. Eustochia. Oh! how two-faced she is! Surely you cannot grasp it. See that she never talks with those who are studying, for pity's sake!4

4. Tell Sr. A. Cleta in my name that I am amazed at how much gossip she managed to spread here in the few hours she stayed.5 Oh! what a tongue from hell! Tell her that if she does not mend her ways I will deal with it myself. Speak to her firmly. Poor wretch, so young, and her tongue so badly infected.

5. For pity's sake look after your health; I add nothing more, as my head is bad. Goodbye, dear Francesca; believe me for all ages

your affectionate M. ROSA

If you need money, write to me; send me the dental instruments.6

Arrangements for Sisters needing sea bathing and for others to be sent to Piacenza.1

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca,

1. Yesterday and today I received no letters from you; I am anxious. Listen, for pity's sake do not leave me without them. Now we must make up for those who lack charity.2

2. Listen, see for yourself which Genoa sisters really need sea baths; bring them to Sestri and send them yourself, having everything bought separately, and see they are well provided for.3

3. Send Sr. A. Eleodora here; tell her she is coming to be divested and send her to the Morte; as for Sr. A., the one with the sores under her arms, if the baths do her no good, send her with the one I say must go to the Morte.4 You understand?

4. I enclose £. 100, and when you run out I will send more; look after your health properly; I long for you to come back, my dear Francesca.

5. Sr. A. Gonzaga is coming for the baths; she too badly needs building up.5

6. I would like to tell you so much more, but if you could see me! Listen, granny is here and longs to see you. They will manage for sleeping; it is hot; some on straw pallets, some on mattresses, won't they?6 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She allows her to renew her vows. Spiritual advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am, ready to grant your request: yes, make your vows,1 for I am delighted.

2. As for Communion,2 you must obey the confessor blindly, without heeding diabolical suggestions. Satan makes it seem that one is doing wrong in order to gain his end. Courage, obedience, obedience, and you will obtain everything.3

In haste, yours,

affectionate M. ROSA

She tells her where the two sisters who have arrived are to go and grants the taking of vows.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. In haste; I am overwhelmed with work. I hear you liked the sisters, but Sr. A. Clemente is for you; the other is for Termini Imerese.

2. So you see I cannot leave her with you as wardrobe-keeper; but if you need a strong one for that house you may take one of the nurses.1 The rest in person.

My regards, and the Archbishop's blessing for me; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

3. Yes, I allow all who have one year of vocation to take the holy

Vows, and the others to renew them.2

She strongly deplores the Superior's lack of charity towards the sick Sisters. She fixes the day for her return to Piacenza and for going back for the bathing cure.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. I hear you are at Sestri. You will have received my registered letter and done what I said.1 Tell that Superior I am truly amazed and unpleasantly surprised at her scant, indeed non-existent, charity.

2. As you know, she tells everyone she would like ladies to come for the baths — and then she has no room for the sisters?!2 Dreadful, viper from hell; whoever has no charity will receive no charity.3

3. I will know how to provide for the poor sisters; if I have no [money] I will go from door to door so that they can be treated. Enough.4 God wills it so, because of my sins!

4. So we shall see each other soon; make sure you are here by the 20th, and then on the 27th you will go back with Nonny, as we have arranged. You will all go [to] Albaro.5 All right, isn't it? Tell your mamma I am not answering her letter because if she saw me she would pity me.

Yesterday my head ached unbelievably. Listen, tell her to come with your sisters; I expect them all, so they can spend a little time with mamma.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. I have just received yours6 and am very sorry to hear you have relapsed. Oh! what a pity; of course, if the baths are not doing you good, come at once, for you can take the cure here too. Do what I say above about the sisters; bring Sr. A. Gemma with you, and Sr. A. Mansueta, whom mamma wants.7 Goodbye,

your affectionate... [M. ROSA]

She has sent a registered letter with £ 100, which must be traced. Various advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am extremely anxious, having sent you £ 100 by registered post with a letter from the Superior Martina inside.1 From the way she behaves one would say it was she who collected it;2 so make enquiries, as I am doing from here; for pity's sake, please.

2. As for coming, God knows how I long to see you, but patience! Your health comes first. So you will be here by the 20th; if you think you can come a few days earlier, do, for you must then go back with Nonny straight after the Saint's feast.3

3. Thank you for the basket; in haste I am yours; look for my letters, for pity's sake.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She regrets that her earlier letters have not arrived and summarizes each of them.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. A line. I gather from your telegram that you have not received the letter. My God! I had put £ 100 in it for what you needed.2 Now Nonny and I have thought that you should go to Federico and he will give you whatever money you need. If only I had done that before!3 But I am sending to the post office now and we shall see.

2. Dear Francesca, be sure it was received, for I already have evidence that someone got it.4 Patience! They play tricks like this on me too!

3. So I see you are not receiving my letters. This is the sixth I have sent.5 In one I said I want a letter every day for news of you, as I am anxious; in another I spoke of the Superiors of Genoa and Sestri and how they must treat the sick. In another I told you to send me Gemma, and also the one who says she is spitting blood, who will be sent home. You see how many have gone astray? In the last I told you to come, since the baths are not doing you good, and that you must go back with Nonny the day after the Saint's feast. Oh, how sad! I told you to bring your mother and sisters.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

The Provincial of the Friars Minor has told her through Fr Rocchi that it is not advisable to send the novices to Italy. She rejects this advice and explains why, repeating the invitation to come with at least one novice.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I reply to yours, received yesterday and dated 12 March, whose expressions reassured me a little.1 So think, and always think, that we have one house, one master, and nothing else, for everything lies in holy union. You understand? I would be against buying a house there. Understand, my daughter, there are some places where I think it unwise to waste money.2

2. Listen, yesterday Fr Rocchi read me a letter from his Provincial telling him to persuade me to give up bringing the novices here.

3. This is what I answered him: "No, I cannot, for that would destroy our institution.3

4.4 The Sisters of Charity do as we do: they send them all to Paris; the Daughters of Mary likewise, all to Genoa." And he said: "But if they do this they will risk being sent away!"4

I replied: "Better one house fewer than a body that is bastard! For it never becomes legitimate in spirit".5

5. Stand firm, for pity's sake, if you want God's blessing.

So courage. Come! This very day I have written to the benefactor and shown him why the novices must come here; and you come, so that with Fr Rocchi here things can be better arranged; I wrote to you a few days ago telling you to come, with Sr. A. Cunegonda in your place for four months.6 So just a little, even a single novice, simply to break the ice.7 It could be the teacher,8 but do as you think best. I will write again soon; I am in such a hurry now, with a world of things to do. Goodbye; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

Tell the sisters I have received their letters and will write to them all when the sisters come; goodbye.

She grants what was asked for the journey to Piacenza. A note on the postulants' dowry.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. For the journey do as you say; I grant everything; likewise for the postulants.1 See that they have at least [£] 300 besides the journey, 250 at the very least,2 always excluding the journey. Goodbye; everything in person,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She commends to her a niece of Fr Rocchi.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive this from Fr Rocchi's hands.1 He would like you to accept his niece, with some reduction2 in the fees. Please do what you can for him; I add nothing more, for I know how great your charity is; I remain your

affectionate M. ROSA

She should send the new postulant in due course. The Sisters are ready. She has received the Sisters' letters and will reply. She is expecting the novices.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply to your two letters; in one you tell me of a rich girl who wants to become a Daughter of Saint Anne — a fine providence; so accept her on condition that she has the money ready to come to Italy as soon as she is clothed, bringing her dowry with her. Oh! tell her I await her with open arms.2 I enclose a letter for the benefactor; please give it to him.

2. I hear you are not very well; I have already written twice telling you to come here and bring me everything,3 but now that I hear you are unwell I tell you not to come, but to look after yourself.

3. Everything is ready here; you cannot believe how good the sisters are; you will be pleased: there is Sr. A. Giuseppina, the Father's niece,4 who knows French, Spanish, English and piano, and is quite something at accounts.

4. Tell the Sisters I have received all their letters, and when the sisters leave I will send replies to each one individually, so they will be pleased and all have a keepsake.

5. I enclose a copy of the contract, and by the August mail I will send another, so that if one goes astray you will have the other.

6. Send me the novices with some sister — if only Amadio could come too!5 — as long as you send some novices; oh! if I could make you understand how much good they bring, you would certainly not have given up. Understood? And more would have entered; enough. For now send what you know, for if you want good Sisters — but you know how much is needed.

7. If you knew how much I have done: the new church, the new novitiate, and building takes money.6 So manage wisely. Goodbye; greetings to all; believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

Very Reverend Vicar,

1. I owe you a thousand apologies for what happened this morning.1 My many occupations and my poor health, which made itself felt more than usual, made me forget what we had agreed, all the more since I had invited you to breakfast with us.2 Forgive me and believe me, with all the respect of this poor wretch, who asks you to bless your most humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She has sent mail through the Consulate. She has doubts about Fr Rocchi, who seems to her tight-fisted towards the Daughters of Saint Anne. Various news and greetings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This morning I sent you one through the Consul, now another; so through the Consul I have sent you an express packet, which you will receive with a letter from me. I enclose a letter for the benefactor, who is (I think he is Bishop Clavijo's brother);1 as I do not have the address, please give it to him; you will see it will do you much good.

2. Now I must tell you a thought of mine, since you and the Sisters have written that you suffered on the voyage because of Fr Rocchi's stinginess. Is that how to provide for the poor sisters? Oh! what a thought! I assure you I really cannot make up my mind; I think I will certainly send them, but I want them well looked after,2 for he is stingy, takes everything for himself and nothing for us. He is always afraid there might be something good for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, and thinks little of them.

3. I hear from your letter that the dispensary is going very well; so I tell you a thought of mine: that the friar in question was behind it, and the same for everything else.3

My dear daughter, you have little experience; that is why you so often think everything is white; trust no one.

4. Tell Sr. A. Cunegonda that her sister is here with us;

she ran away from home as she did; her uncle, her mamma's brother, sent to look for her, but without fuss, and I hope they will calm down and everything can be settled; she need not worry.4 Her sister is happy and cheerful and well, as are all her family. I will write to her another time, so that the Sisters can bring it.

5. I have sent you two copies of the contracts; I hope you have received them, as well as my letter where I told you many things about those sisters, or rather the postulant, whom I accept provided she comes here; with one, another may follow.5

6. Goodbye; we are so busy; on 15 August the sister Superiors are coming to hold a General Chapter for certain decisions, of which you will be informed as soon as they are made, and you may send your vote if you wish.6

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters; they will receive letters from me by the sisters' hands; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She encourages her to overcome difficulties, advising her from personal experience to carry each day's cross and to give no weight to "gossip". She should look after her health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear from your letter of your troubles, so many that they are harming your health; this upsets me greatly and grieves me.1 Ah! what are you doing?

2. Listen, my dear daughter, you must do as I do every day: new days, so new crosses. In the evening I take mine and carry it to Jesus; the next day, as it is new, I press it to my heart, kiss it and then go on.

3. I pay no attention to gossip. Do you know what I say? Whoever talks behind my back is talking to my back; it cannot hear, and it is broad enough to hear nothing.2 So be cheerful and do not be afraid.3

4. I cannot tell you much of what is being done, for you will hear it in person. Cheer up, for I am here and keep a good pace; you know I am a giant at suffering! I challenge everyone — and you lose heart? No! Look after your health, for pity's sake.

Bring Sr. A. Rosaria with you;4 I have received everything, thank you,5 and believe me ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is glad of the good news of the journey and everyone's wellbeing. Advice on her health.

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca,

1. Today I have no letter from you; yesterday I received the one telling me about the journey, how you all are, and what you have done. I hear Nonny is enjoying herself and has an appetite. Oh! dear Jesus, if only we could see her free of the cough for once!1

2. Poor uncles, how good they are to us! I assure you it gave me great pleasure.2 Try to get well, so that you will be strong enough to fight.

I add only that you should write to me every day; I also want to know if you need anything.

Goodbye; I am truly worn out with work; eternally your affectionate M. ROSA

She tells her of the croup epidemic that has killed many children. Advice and greetings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your letter this morning; I assure you it was most dear to me, as were Gaspare's and Nonny's. Oh! how dreadful, dear Francesca, if she were still here! Oh! how the croup is raging! Mariani, Franzoli, Borrelli, Permetti — these in just two days; it is a massacre.1 Everyone is fleeing; it is desolation.

2. For pity's sake do not take Nonny about; I do not much like your going to Sestri by tram; tell Gaspare it is better for her to stay put. Bathing tires Nonny too much. It is pleasant in that square at Albaro, and she need not go gadding about. You understand? Ices together with bathing are not advisable; in short, take care.

3. Granny is very well, getting stronger day by day; she goes right up to the top of the garden in one go, and has even been out; I assure you I am really well.2

4. For pity's sake look after yourselves and believe me yours; let Gaspare read this. Goodbye; greetings to the uncles and my sister-in-law, and to Nonny, whom I thank for her letter;3 let her always write to me; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

Several children have died of diphtheria or croup. It is unwise to bring Nonny back to Piacenza. She should stay on; then we shall see.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I gather from your letter of yesterday that you have still received neither the telegram nor the letter telling you that diphtheria and croup are raging here in Piacenza. How many children are dying! For pity's sake do not bring Nonny, no! no!

2. Rather stay wherever you think best, [at] Albaro or wherever Gaspare thinks, and when you have to be here2 another nun will go there, whichever Gaspare thinks best, together with him, for it is not wise. Oh! what a massacre! It seems Nonny foresaw it, for she wanted nothing but to leave.

3. So, for pity's sake, do not move, and in this heat do not take her about, for the heat may harm her. Stay wherever you like. Carla is well; she is here writing.

Goodbye; show this to Gaspare, whom I greet; a kiss to Nonny; and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

She will send the money for the daily Masses. Receipts should be sent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I take the opportunity to reply through Francesco. The Masses will begin on 1 October, as that suits me.1 I need to know the Chaplain's name, and he will send me the receipts, for I too must hand them over.2

You are right about providence.3 What a sorrow for me too!

Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has heard from the doctor about the course of the epidemic and the children's deaths. She advises them not to move. News of herself and Carla. Advice.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

1. A line to tell you I received both your letters this morning; last night I was rather anxious. I am pleased to hear you are putting on weight and that Nonny is in fine form. Oh! what a grace we owe the Lord for what he did for Nonny!

2. Listen, if Gaspare wants to come, let him, and you can stay with Nonny; then you need only be here for the Chapter, and Gaspare would go back there.

3. Not here!1 Oh! what a massacre; I have just been speaking with Albertazzi, and he says it is something new: it comes on exactly as with poor Rosetto; the croup comes, then with an emetic they bring it up,2 they seem cured, and then severe diphtheria sets in with a return of the croup, which chokes them.3

4. Look, just among those we know: Meroni, Ratti, another near Ratti, and Franzoli, and two more in Guastafredda, towards the station. Buzelli Guarà's, and another this morning, the doctor tells me; even Gaspare's doctor lost his little one.4 They have not managed to save a single one; no, all [have died]. Meroni brought professors from everywhere; they operated on her. Oh! what agony!!!

5. Tell Gaspare whether this is nonsense. Far from it! Clearly Nonny foresaw this terrible crisis. Granny too. She says: for pity's sake, she must not come; since you are safe, stay there, for pity's sake.

6. Carla is well; I do what I can. She seems content; she only misses Gaspare, but is glad to think Nonny is not here, which would be a great worry. For pity's sake look after yourself; don't eat rich pastries.

7. Here it is so hot one cannot breathe; never any rain; everyone is frightened.5 So be cheerful and believe me yours, and Gaspare's and the whole family's.

Please send back the basket the chickens came in, as it is not ours and the Sanacavallo woman wants it; try to send it. Did you get the goose? Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to act for the Superior. Various instructions for the task.1

A.M.F.2

My daughter,

1. Until the Superior arrives you will act in her place.3 I urge observance, meditation, prayer.

2. These are the keys to every good; and if you want Providence, have the girls pray: a novena to the Saint, to St Joseph, and to St Francis of Paola. In short, pray.

3. Tell the teacher I expect her soon.4 I commend the girls to you; I look forward to good news.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you. I am your affectionate M. ROSA

Greet all the Sisters, the girls and the teacher for me.

1. In acknowledging receipt of your esteemed letter cited in the margin,1 I offer my warmest thanks for the kindness with which you judge the poor works of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

2. They deserve no praise of any kind, and if your Honorable Administration is pleased to appreciate their labors, that is owing to its own goodness.

With my respects, I remain your most illustrious Lordship's
