She thanks her and hopes she is well.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. With the greatest pleasure I received your dear letter. Endless thanks, my poor child!2 I would like to hear you are a little stronger in health. Goodbye; yours in my dear Crucified Lord,

affectionate M. ROSA

She replies to her letter with advice on running the house, where she has recently arrived.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I learn everything from your letter; that is what comes of one wretched woman!2 What trouble! Listen, if by misfortune that priest3 dared tell you to leave, tell him you are not leaving at all; let him go; you are in your own house and he has nothing to do with it; be firm.4 I hope it will not happen, but I am warning you just in case, so that you will be strong.

Goodbye; in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She should send the sisters out collecting alms and give money to no one.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you to send the sisters out collecting at once. And send no money to anyone, nothing to Don Francesco;2 let him talk; he came here and took £ 50 from me. What a bungler!3 Enough; in person; God willing I will come.

2. Tell the alms-collectors I expect them on their round, as I need to speak to Sr. A. Pierina about some business of hers.

Goodbye; courage,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Greet all the sisters.

Yesterday Don Francesco left for Genoa to see the Cardinal,4 giving me to understand he was going to Milan. Oh! how many lies!

She apologizes for moving a Sister from the Pignatelli Institute, of which he is President, without notice.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I cannot express all my sorrow at having displeased Your Most Reverend Excellency, from whom I have received so many proofs of charity and to whom I am bound by the liveliest gratitude. I trust, however, that once you have heard what I have to say you will be persuaded that my fault towards Your Excellency was involuntary, and will deign to forgive it. The transfer of Sr. A. Clemente was proposed to me by Sr. A. Crocifissa, and I thought you consented.1

2. I took care to choose the sister to replace her from among the most skilled, and I can assure you that the one I sent works and draws excellently; I have no other who surpasses her in needlework.2

3. While I thought I was doing something pleasing to Your Excellency, I hear you were displeased, which grieves me not a little; I am ready, whenever you wish, to restore things as they were.3

4. Is Your Excellency not the master of your own orphanage? Please therefore tell me your wishes, which I shall fully respect. You will find me most obedient to your every sign, since Your Excellency deserves all my obedience and respect.

5. Hoping that Your Excellency will forgive my involuntary fault, I beg you to make known your will and to bless her who, prostrate at your feet, remains

Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most devoted Servant

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She cannot send the teacher but has a Sister pianist available. She thinks the Superior could take on the role of visitor for Sicily. She must go to Linguaglossa, but after the examinations.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have another letter from you and hear the councillors are expecting the teacher I mentioned in the telegram; but having had no reply from them I have used the diploma-holder elsewhere; I could send a good pianist [who knows] French and Spanish, but without a diploma;2 it seems to me that one — indeed they have three qualified ones — is that not enough?

2. I think it could be done as you say; try to settle things well and calm down, and see about the examinations. Listen, I hope Jesus really wants to see a little order, so as to send us peace.

3. Listen, I think it could be done like this: you remain visitor for Sicily, going from house to house and always on the move.3 Now there is Linguaglossa — if you knew how it grieves me! My God, what a business!4 You would need to go there (not now), but once the examinations are over there; then you could take Savina along for a little distraction and leave Sr. A. Cecilia for those few days.5 What do you say? Ah! if only the examinations were over! Patience! Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She learns with regret of the house's deficit. She cannot act at once as she is about to leave, but will call her on her return.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I read your letter late, as I was in bed. I hear with the greatest regret of the debts incurred.1 My God! A house that was doing so well, and now I must see it like this! What am I to do, when at this moment I really do not know what to say? If you saw things here you would say: "poor Mother!"

2. So, if you [can] use your ingenuity, we will then see each other.2 I would call you, but I leave tomorrow; I will let you know on my return.3 I urge observance. For pity's sake, cling to the Crucifix, where I hold you every day.

Greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She warns her about Don Francesco's behavior. She must always act prudently and shrewdly.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Do not believe Don Francesco's falsehoods at all. Ah! the things he says and does! He certainly harms himself, for truth is queen of the world, and so, poor man, he becomes more and more a laughing stock!1

2. So be firm! Let him say Mass and then go; if he has debts, let him pay them, but you will give him nothing more. What he says about the Cardinal has so far been all lies.2

3. Sr. A. Domenica will never come to Bassano again; stand firm, for his way of acting robs the Institute and the poor Sisters of their good name.3 How dreadful! I assure you it makes me feel truly ill to see such ugly things; in reality there will be nothing in it, but the wicked world judges everything ill and is scandalized.

4. What must we do? We must remove anything that could give scandal.4 Firm: Mass and then off at once, no corale (?), don't waste time.5 You are capable and shrewd enough, and I am pleased with you.

5. Please be very shrewd during the Holy Exercises,6 for I am very afraid. Goodbye; read this as best you can, for I am in a hurry,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Thanks. The Sister will arrive.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Your dear letter was most welcome; you cannot believe how I blessed God for it. Irmina will soon be with you, as I have written to her to come.2

Goodbye; yours in my dear Crucified Lord.

Affectionate M. ROSA

She tells her about paying an expense that the Mother will cover.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Do nothing about the grapes; I will send from here.1 I hope you have settled everything with the Administration, so that there will be no more friction.2

Goodbye; greetings to all the sisters; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

A clear lesson in humility about offices. An exhortation to prudence.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How it displeases me to read in your letter that you cannot bring yourself to give orders to a sister who has already been superior! Oh! what an ugly thing to say! So if we have been superiors we can no longer bring ourselves to obey? What nonsense! No, we are all equal: one day superior and another day dishwasher.1

2. Oh! I did that job for many years; would to God it fell to me again before I die; I would be most fortunate.

3. So, for pity's sake, do not go to law; it is better to keep quiet in these circumstances, for these people have nothing to lose; I beg you, silence!2 Sure that you will do as I say, I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

It was the Spirit of God who prompted her to defend his Work. He used a donkey for his glory; and for his Work Jesus has used her, a poor, ignorant sinner, good only at spoiling things, yet seized by one desire alone: to see her daughters holy. So let her stand firm in defending and conducting the affairs of the Lord's Work.1

A.JVl.r.

My daughter,

1. I received your dear registered letter. You ask me what spirit made you speak! My God! Tell me: "Are you convinced that what you are dealing with is God's Work? Are you convinced that what you say is to defend the Institute and help it grow?2 And to defend it from the enemy legions? Yes?" Well then, for his own good and glory Jesus made a donkey speak to the Prophet,3 and likewise for his Work — do you not see whom Jesus has used? A poor, ignorant sinner like me. It is truly so: I have nothing but humiliation at seeing myself so incapable of doing a little good, good only at spoiling things.4

2. And tell me: "Do you believe I want only one thing, your sanctification? Yes, isn't it true?" Well, wretch that I am, I never cease to ask my God, through the merits of my dear Crucified Lord, to sanctify you all, as I cling to him in my poor room. Oh! how strongly I hold you in his heart! Oh! sweet love!5

3. Yes, my dear daughter, seek me in him, and I promise you will always find me; I promise. Yes, Jesus will put on your tongue words that even you will not know how you came to say!6 And if you always stand firm in wanting to defend and vigorously conduct the affairs of the Lord's Work, you will see, I promise, that one day you will feel the benefit. More: before leaving this life you will experience great things; your heart will enjoy heavenly love in union with that dear, sweet Love!

4. Ah! Enough, I fear I am saying too much: my nature is such that, seeing myself so ugly, misshapen and inept, my soul trembles with confusion! Love, and think that it was Jesus speaking in your heart, and you were his echo, another self.7

5. Humility and obedience — said Jesus to a soul — and for the rest you will have all you need; fear nothing. The devil fears rif.ento (?) the humble soul, and whoever is humble also has charity, a beautiful treasure!8 Love it! Tell me, what would you do for charity? Ah! how I hunger for it!

6. Last night I dreamed of her. Oh! What did I feel?! I am old now and cannot say I have been able to taste even a little of this most dear and sweet beloved of mine.9

7. I would like to draw the whole world, give to everyone, feed everyone. Oh! [if] I could make gold flow from my veins for the poor, do you know what I would do? I would draw it out myself, vein by vein, until they ran dry. Oh! would I be satisfied? No! It is too ardent!10

8. Goodbye; I hold you close in the Heart of Jesus, always ready to be with you whenever you want me.

The Cardinal is still in Genoa; as soon as I know he has left I will write, so that you can go at once. Tell me, did you mention that your observations were not signed by me?11 For you say nothing in your letter. Goodbye, your [affectionate M. ROSA]

She asks for news, gives her travel schedule, and adds instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. First of all, I was expecting news from there today and got none; I fear you did not put Bellinzago Novarese and so it went astray; for pity's sake, if anything is wrong, telegraph me.

2. Tomorrow I spend all day at Varallo Pombia, and the day after at 10 I shall be at Legnano; I will stay all day and night there and leave early for Milan. If you are all well — Carla, Nonny, you — telegraph me at Legnano so that I can be easier; then I go to Bregnano, [staying] only a day, and then I will be straight [with you]; I am coming home.

3. So send Sr. A. Giacomina off to Mercatello; I enclose her obedience papers so that she can go at once, for I had promised to send her as early as Monday. Tell her to put that house in good order, and then Sr. A. Carmelita will come down.1

4. Have the alms-collectors arrived? I am anxious! For pity's sake, if only I could know something, and about the letters too, but how?2 I hope there is nothing urgent; if so you can always telegraph me at Legnano.

5. I do urge you to have someone sleep in the Father's room; you will understand why, won't you? Have the windows shut properly; for pity's sake keep watch at night.3

Goodbye; greetings to Carla and Gaspare, Nonny and all the sisters; receive a thousand ... in the Heart of Jesus; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She asks for news and tells her about two Sisters due to arrive in Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the certificate and hope you have received my long letter;1 I would like to know what you have done about the Princess's house.2

2. If the sister teacher has reached you from Naples, for pity's sake keep a close eye on her and send her to me at the first opportunity;3 if she behaves badly, send her alone. If someone from Montalto has brought you a Sister, keep her there and I will send her on later; meanwhile make use of her.4 Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA In two days I shall be in Piacenza.

She is not to leave the "Pignatelli". Sr. A. Olga is to have a notary draw up a power of attorney. She must not keep both teachers.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. So stay at the Pignatelli and let no more be said, or there will be a mess. Pulling this way and that, people get upset; carry on.2

2. Tell Sr. A. Olga that the power of attorney must be legal and made out to Sr. A. Benedetta, but in her lay name, Marchioness Carrega Anna daughter of Antonio, legally; this was the form she was to give the lawyer drawing it up.3

3. Goodbye; I am in a hurry. You ask to keep both teachers; that is too much for you alone; remember I cannot send others; take the one who cannot work as a nurse. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

Various news. She will entrust to the sisters what was asked for. She hopes to open another house in America.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. It is true I let several mails go by without writing,1 for I was so busy I had not a minute free, and meanwhile I was hoping the sisters would come; but Fr Rocchi is slow in coming, so I see he will not leave until mid or late November;2 that is why I am writing.

2. No doubt that person will have come to you with my letters; you will have heard what he said and so been able to do what you mention.3 I don't know; it was truly a grace of the Lord that he sent me this person. So you will be pleased, won't you?

3. So I hear one must now say that someone was acting as trumpeter at the time,4 but all by God's permission, who, if he does this, does it for our good. Oh! the Lord's goodness in doing this, so that we may gain some merit.

4. Certainly dear Jesus has been badly treated by the Americans.5 They went there to edify, and instead [of] edifying you have scandalized; I do not mean you, but the poor sisters — or rather, silly little things. All their sacrifice has done them no good, for they have soiled it all disgracefully. They were to build up and they have destroyed.6

5. As soon as the sisters come I will send you everything you want.

I am now having a very large novitiate built, with 250 beds; I have built the new church, bought a fine house in Florence, and will send you the list of houses opened. I also hope to open one at [...]; the final answer is now coming. Oh! yes, it would surely be a great good for you to have sisters nearby! I won't give the name, for you are women's tongues, and I don't think it wise to say it; it is enough to say it is in America.7

6. I will send you everything with the sisters who are coming. One of them is qualified, all right? She plays, knows French, is very young, but an angel who truly does not know how to gossip. I would not want her to have to learn.8

Goodbye; yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

She received her letter with joy and comfort. She blesses her, asks for prayers and promises them.1

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. A line in reply to yours,2 and rest assured that your happiness is mine; you cannot believe what a comfort it is to hear you are content.3

2. Oh! may God pour his blessings abundantly on your head and make you a great Saint.

3. Pray hard for me; yes, my dear daughter, by prayer we obtain everything. Remember that I always put the Americans first in all my prayers, so that Jesus may keep them healthy and holy for me.4

Goodbye; yours in my dear Crucified Lord.

Affectionate M. ROSA

She answers the Superior's questions with precise directions: pay no earlier debts, give away none of the house furnishings that belong to us. She has written to the lawyer about the situation. Advice about the confessor.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say. Listen, in two words: do not commit yourself, for pity's sake, to paying old bills, no!1 Oh! if only I could talk to you! Oh! daughter, stand firm with that wretched priest. Oh! let us pray!

2. So do nothing. Listen, the room you sleep in was given by a lady, as was all the table linen and many other things.2

3. And then, listen, I enclose a copy of the money we gave him; so he must take nothing; first let him return our money. I have already had the lawyer write.3

4. As for giving him the present, yes, do so, but I urge you not to be alone for a minute; keep to what I wrote.4

5. I enclose a list of items, but you see, not everything is there. Meanwhile stand firm; they must touch nothing.

6. I hear about the confessor. Abolish all the abuses, which we do not allow anywhere.5 Oh! how sad what you tell me; for pity's sake be like bronze.

Listen, tell me whether you have an extraordinary confessor, so that I can find him at once; then, by speaking with him,6 I hope Saint Anne will see to it.

7. I sympathize; it is certainly a great trial, poor child, but you will see that Jesus will see to it. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is not to handle the negotiations with Princess Odescalchi, who wants Fr Agostino Donadio as mediator.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to acknowledge receipt of your letters. Blessed be God in all things, who does everything for our greater good.

2. Listen, since the Princess says she wants Fr Agostino, drop all negotiations and tell her Fr Agostino will come.1 Do you know why? I do not like what she wants at all.2 I will not strip one house to clothe another.

3. Listen, I have written to the Protector and will write to you.3 Meanwhile I send you a copy of the letter Boccali wrote me on behalf of the Holy Father.4 It will please you.

4. Forgive me for writing so little, but I am truly overwhelmed with work. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

Explanations about a legal power of attorney. She asks that the Administration pay the Sisters' travel.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, the form sent to Sr. A. Olga is for drawing up a legal power of attorney. You must call a notary and give him the paper, and he will draw it up legally; have I explained?1 For the rest, I am glad to hear everything went well; thanks be to God!

2. [For] the three sisters I sent to the new house2 they have not paid me the full travel costs; so I would like you to do the sums and kindly have everything sent to me, including the journey of the one still to come, the teacher.3

3. If you knew how much I have to spend on these journeys! My God! It is appalling.

Greetings to all, and believe me ever your affectionate M. ROSA

She comforts her, encouraging her to go forward joyfully amid troubles, which she shares with affection and understanding.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear of your troubles and am sorry;1 alas, dear daughter, this is what comes of the disorders of a wretched creature who, instead of being attached to her Institute, betrays it and does all manner of things! Oh! what sorrows! you cannot believe it!2

2. Listen, do not worry about what you gave, for there is no harm in it. What I wrote was for your guidance and nothing more, so that you will know how to act.3

3. Courage like a giant, for it is truly needed at this time!

4. I have put myself in the lawyer's hands, for I see there is no getting anywhere with people of this sort.4 You did well about the alms-collectors.5

5. Listen, a qualified teacher is coming now; I am half thinking of sending your cousin. She is happy and seems to like it here. Once she is clothed I would send her to you, and you could be her teacher and teach her many things; then there would be nothing more to say about the diploma, would there?

6. Keep your spirits up and be cheerful, for pity's sake, for I am always with you in your needs and troubles, sharing in everything, your affectionate M. ROSA

She had better return to the Parrocchietta, and the school in Via delle Fornaci should reopen. She names the Sisters to be assigned to the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You had better go to the Parrocchietta and leave Margana.1 Fr Agostino will come in two days and will see to everything. You must look after the Fornaci; while it is idle you can send Sr. A. Paola there as acting Superior, or your cook, Sr. A. Giacobba, who may [accept] if she knows she is to stay only until the teacher and Superior arrive.

2. But now its opening must not be delayed any longer; send three there at once. Meanwhile Sr. A. Giacobba, who can write a little, can enter the children in the register in rough.2 For pity's sake do it at once.

3. Fr Agostino will bring the teacher and Superior, but you go to the Parrocchietta at once, and the others to the Fornaci. You can take whomever you like as cook for the time being, can't you? I have received your letter.

In haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She grants what was asked. A Sister is to go to Ferrara with the alms-collectors.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about Domenica's things. Listen, you may use them all;1 as for the sister taking a little coffee, yes, and other things too; as for the one wanting America, no.2

2. Listen, please do me the kindness of sending Sr. A. Babila to Ferrara while the alms-collectors are passing. When your cousin is clothed I will send her to you; all right? are you pleased?3 For now another can stay [with] the girls, whichever you think best. I am sure you will do as I ask, since it is for the good of the Ferrara boarding school.

3. If you want more sisters, I can send them. I await a letter from you; I wrote yesterday. I am your

affectionate M. ROSA

I also allow that lady to come to your chapel.4

Moved by her words, she urges her to spend herself entirely for Jesus. The Sisters will arrive.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

1. A line in the greatest haste, for I am so weighed down with work. Oh! how true it is that great patience is needed! But for Jesus everything is little; it is [for] that sweet Love, yes! For him, everything.1

2. Your letter and your words moved me. No, you must tell Jesus that for him you want to work until death and spend yourself entirely, but not what you ask of me, no.2 Jesus is pleased with the desire, and I assure you he has accepted it; so, for your comfort, you have done everything well.

3. Fr Agostino will tell you the rest and bring the teacher and Superior for the Fornaci, so Sr. A. Giacobba3 will return to her kitchen with you. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received reports on the house. She approves what has been done, advises on what to do next, and urges her not to overtire herself and to take care.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about the house and how tiring it is.2 For pity's sake don't overtire yourself. Before anything else I want you to look after your health.

2. As for the kitchen, that is fine; do as you say; I spoke to the Father and he said it can be done that way.3

3. As for the schools, patience is needed. Oh! how dreadful! A Superior who, instead of working for the good of the Institute, pulls towards ...;4 so things must be left as they are, the boarding school too.

4. As for the examinations, better not mention them again;5 you will hold them next year, always fixing them for early July as the school regulations say, so that you can both go and take a few baths.

5. You can have Sr. A. Savina do everything; she will get used to it, and one day she could be relied on.6 So don't tire yourself out; let her do all the tiring work.7 Take care of yourself, for pity's sake. In haste,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She disapproves of what she has done and asks for news of a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about Sr. A. Speciosa. For pity's sake let it not happen again.1 Otherwise you tell me nothing. If she is now calm, how is she? I hope everything will be settled and that you will worry no more.2

I would like to tell you so many things, but I am overwhelmed with work; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

Greetings to all the sisters. I am [affectionate M. ROSA]

She answers some questions. The agreement with the gardener about his obligations to the Sisters must be made quite clear. Various advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply at once: 1st, as for the harmonium, patience now; let no more be said; let him keep it! I don't want you to be upset, but take everything from God's hands.1 2nd, you did very well about the maize.2 3rd, now you must tell the gardener that if he takes away anything from the garden, or for the cows, he will be held responsible, and woe to him if he gives anything to the Chemin family; he must give everything to you.

2. And find out how matters stand with that gardener and take the accounts yourself; it is time to put an end to this. Oh! what troubles one must go through because of that wretched man!

3. As for the firewood, buy it, and the grapes for wine too. I approve everything, and I hope the alms-collectors, coming soon, will be a great help. On Monday two nuns will set out for your house. That means you may keep the 88 £ the gardener gave Signor Biagio, as well as the wine he gave you.3

4. For the rest, see that they take nothing. Oh! the things one has to see!4 As for Mass, have another priest say it.5 Goodbye; yours for all ages, affectionate M. ROSA

Ready to obey the summons to Rome but prevented by serious ill health. She will go as soon as possible.

Most Reverend Eminence

1. His Excellency the Bishop of Piacenza has passed on to me Your Most Reverend Eminence's letter summoning me there.1

2. I would not hesitate a moment to obey you, were it not for my poor health; were I to undertake such a journey I am sure I would have to stop half way and could go no further.2

I therefore beg Your Most Reverend Eminence to believe that as soon as I am able to come I shall hasten to present myself at your feet.3

Grant me your Pastoral Blessing; I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's humble and most devoted Servant SISTER ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

She asks her to take in a girl.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, please do me the kindness of keeping the girl whom the Superior Sr. A. Martina will hand over to you, for three months only; I will take her back on my return from the visit.2

Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received the letter to be delivered and will see to it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am so busy I don't know where to begin on the immense tasks I have.1 I have received yours enclosing M. R.'s letter, which I will hand to the Marchioness2 as soon as she returns from Milan, or rather have the Father hand it to her;3 she is unwell and under the care of a Milanese doctor.4 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to organize the finances of the "Ardizzone" Institute better, entrusting the spending to another Sister.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A hurried line, as I am overwhelmed with work. So I hear what the young lady did! My God!2 So much preaching, so many exhortations, and where have they ended up? Enough; to the point.

2. Let her hear this order of mine. I no longer want her to have money; you will take charge of it all, and Sr. A. Clemente will do the buying; she is to be mistress of nothing, nothing.3 That is what I want. I wish you to see it carried out.

Otherwise all is well. Courage; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She commends her for reporting certain failings in the community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Be at peace, for nothing was said; I only hope it will not happen again, and if you see anything, remember you are bound by holy obedience to write and tell me.1

2. Ah! how beautiful this jewel is! I would like to tell you so many things, but if you saw how much I have to do!

Ah! I am tired, it is late and I really feel [ill]; I can do no more!2

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks her for what she sent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A thousand thanks for what you sent me, though I have not yet received it.1 I hope it will arrive safely.

2. I am very sorry about that man, but don't take it to heart;2 you will see it will all end and be settled; I hold you close in my Jesus; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks her and urges her to take care of herself.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Thank you for all you sent through Sr. A. Berta.2 I hear you are still thin. Oh! look after your health; it will be a real comfort to me.

Receive a warm embrace in my dear Crucified Lord. I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She has failed to obtain the hoped-for financial help for Mgr Ricci.

A.M.F

My daughter,

1. A line in haste: clearly the Lord makes everything I try to do for Mgr Ricci fail; not even the Marchioness Negrone — she has gone another way.1 Oh! what troubles! Patience; if the Lord permits it, he surely has his just purposes.

2. So forgive me if I write no more; I am so overwhelmed; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She was comforted to know she is content and hopes she will settle in the new house. She encourages her to love the cross of Jesus.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you have passed from gloom to cheerfulness. Oh! what a sweet comfort that was for me! Yes, daughter, you want to go to Egypt? Well, your wish will be granted!1

2. You know I have always done what you wanted; I hope you will now be happy there; I await your letter.2

3. Oh! Cross, how dear you are, and yet refused by all! Do you know what I say to Jesus? Give me all the crosses of the Daughters of Saint Anne, for whoever does not love the cross [shows] that she loves Jesus little. Isn't that so? So come, let us become saints. All the rest is pure illusion and nothing more.

Goodbye; in great haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She explains the reason for the transfer, with words of affection and exhortation.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. From your letter received last night I see you are unhappy at having come there. Oh! how could it even enter my head that you went to that house as a punishment?!!2 Oh! daughter, how can that be?

2. Tell me: to a place where I send only the very best — I am so anxious for the Institute to be well thought of, and it is the good members who make it so, isn't it? my God!3

3. And could I possibly try to punish one of my dearest daughters without saying anything to her?

4. My Irene, for pity's sake, do well, and then you will go to Egypt.4

I am in haste; I look for good news, for if you knew how weighed down with troubles I am!

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received the letter repaying the travel costs. She asks for prayers and gives advice about a Sister. She is about to go to Genoa and then to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I gather from your letters that the Devil is making war in that house; a good sign.1 I hope Sr. A. Irene has received my letter and settled down. My God! I have no one else.

2. Listen, you ask whether I received the registered letter; as soon as it came I wrote to tell you I had received the one with the sisters' travel money; I assure you I spent more, for they insisted on traveling second class. My God! If you knew how I am placed! What troubles! Pray and have others pray; the building is nearly finished!

3. Back to Irene: if you go and see she is not doing well, send her to Naples.

4. I would like to tell you so many things, but I am so overwhelmed with work; moreover today I must go to Genoa, then come back here and leave at once for Rome, where ... enough;2 God willing I will tell you everything in person.

I am yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

She encourages her to see the bright side of things and the fruits of the cross and of trials. She asks for prayers.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. A line in haste, for I am in the midst of a world of business. My God! Listen, my daughter, after bad weather comes the sun; be at peace, for very beautiful flowers will blossom in your house.2

2. Yes! I have no doubt: where there are the cross and trials, do you know what happens? The tree grows ever firmer. Courage, you will see, and one day you will bear out what I tell you.3

3. Pray that Jesus may give me strength to bear everything, and, God willing, I will come there too.4 For pity's sake do not lose heart; keep your spirits up, for you will see the devil flee and the dear little angels stay to keep you company.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

Approval and advice.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste; your letter comforted me so much; well done, daughter! Listen, have that work done,2 and God will send you Providence; send the alms-collectors out on their round at once and they will bring you something; but from what you say it is a necessity, so do it.3

2. Accept the postulant, with the £ 500 and the little trousseau she has. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She cannot see why she doubts her affection and motherly concern. She urges her to look after her health and explains why she was placed in the new work in Palermo.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. As soon as I read it I reply, though I am immersed in work. Ah! how it grieves me to see you doubt that my affection has lessened! Your words: "she was always a mother to me...".1 Ah! what a thought to have, and on what do you base it? My God!

2. This is the third letter I have written; I would like to know whether you received it; from them you can see whether I am right or not to find this doubt of yours ill-sounding — I would not know what to call it.2 What do you say, what are you doing?

3. You tell me your health is failing; how can that be? Woe to you if it did! Do you know what I will do? I will take a whip and beat you until you get well! A remedy? Ah! joking aside!3 After your health has cost me so much, will you gamble it away for nothing? Well done — so much for going to Egypt!4

4. Listen, if I sent you there it was because I hoped that you, who always did so well with the girls, would be the only one able to put that house in good order, and I ask you to do so. I won't add how, for God has given you spirit enough to get out of any difficulty.5

Write to me and let me know you have received my letters. Goodbye for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

Give me your address.6

Various instructions. She asks whether she wants a Sister moved.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Now it is a fine mess, for I have no teacher left; what am I to do? My God!1 As for having paid her journey, that can certainly not be right; it would have been better for her to pay it, since with what she earns she wrote that she would cover all expenses; besides, you are so poor!2 Patience! Please pay the debts.

2. I have had complaints that you are often in Lugo and that it is not right; the priests were surprised. For pity's sake do not go about, for these are such nasty towns that they remark on everything. Oh! what trouble! So don't go there any more.

3. As for Sr. A. Amabile, if you think fit I will change her and send you another, but I fear she will not be so good at cutting out; at embroidery, yes, she is skilled, in gold too.3

4. I await your letters; we will talk better in person, for I hope to be in Bologna by the 24th. You will be told by telegram; but about Amabile I want an answer at once, so that I can use her elsewhere.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She is pleased with her work and commends the sick Sisters to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am very glad to tell you I am pleased with what you are doing; that is all. As for the sisters, give this letter to Sr. A. Fiorentina to read to them.1 Tell the alms-collectors that what they did is forgiven, but they must not do it again.2 Greetings to the Canon3 and to all the sick, whom I commend to you as if they were myself,4 and also the daughter of the woman from Nice; see that she studies and learns cleanliness, please. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She is sorry to hear of a Sister's discontent and advises treating her kindly and tactfully. She leaves for Rome on the 22nd.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am very sorry to hear that the sister is not behaving as you would like, but I hope that, having received my letter, she has settled down. Remember I have no one to send you.2

2. Listen, she tells me she wanted to move the school upstairs, and from what she says it seems a good idea, doesn't it?3 What do you say? For as things are now (if it is as she says!) the friar hears everything, so I think it would be better.

3. So look kindly at this creature. You know she is very good with girls and in school; moreover you must handle her gently, for she is like a child.4 You know we all have faults; so what can we do? We must bear with them.5 I thought it well to describe her character to you.

4. I await your letters anxiously; for your information, I leave on the 22nd and, God willing, will be in Rome by the first of December. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

Advice on escorting three postulants to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Send the three postulants, if you intend to send the alms-collecting sisters to Milan.1 If you have someone you know, fine; otherwise you should know that the Sisters go. I am not sure I am doing right, but they could accompany them as far as here and then go elsewhere.2 I leave you to do what is best.

2. I want the postulants at once. If the journey would not harm you, you could bring them yourself, and we could talk about the money Don Francesco mentions.3 Remember I leave on the 20th.4 Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She refuses an administrative request. The Superior should ask the administrators to pay at least a fourth Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your registered letter; all right. As for doing what you say about the girls' food, it cannot and must not be done at all.1 Rather keep after the councillors to pay at least one more;2 otherwise you may keep the girls' fees, yes,3 but not that.

Goodbye; I am about to leave; goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She will send the money. The alms-collectors may go to Milan.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply in haste to tell you that before Christmas I will send £ 300: 100 for you and 200 for the Bishop, so that he can give something to the house's people.1

2. Now one thing: you may send your alms-collectors to Milan, for I have withdrawn the others and they have not been there for a year.2

For the rest I pray for you all; do the same; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She dispels rumors about a Sister and gives news of her. She asks about the other communities in Crotone.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Although I am overwhelmed with work — so many houses to open, sisters leaving for America, and I myself due to go on visitation to Tuscany on the 22nd of this [month] and then straight on to Rome — to show how welcome your letter with such good news was, I write a line to refute more surely what your confessor told you.1

2. It is all utterly false: that sister is at Ferrara teaching sewing to the boarders, and is very happy to be there (as she herself puts it, "under a good superior and dear sisters"), now that the boarding school has grown; it is truly a pleasure to see, and the whole city is delighted with it.

3. She [is] there with the other teachers — three qualified and two without diplomas — all assigned to that boarding school, which is a high-class one.

4. See the lies; I do not believe the Archbishop said all this,2 for he knows everything and is too holy an Archbishop; he would certainly not have allowed the slightest thing to be done. Oh! what nonsense!! Stories people go about telling here and there!

5. I would like to know how those at the Nursery School are behaving, what is said of them there, and of those at the Foundling Hospital.3 You can address letters here.

6. Goodbye; pray and have others pray for me, for I am not very well, that I may have strength for this journey! Pray also for a certain person (it is me); greetings to the superior and the sisters; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

She is to send the four postulants on to Palermo.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, four postulants will reach you; keep them a few days, then send them to Palermo, to the nurses' house. The ad dress is: Daughters of Saint Anne, at the house of the Boccone del Povero,

Padre Bova, IO.1

I will also write to that Superior, so that she can find a way of sending them to me.2

2. Take care of yourself and be strong as a giant; take every precaution.3 Greetings to all the Sisters; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her comforting letter and approves her work. She advises sending the savings towards the cost of enlarging the Mother House.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter was a great comfort to me;1 always do as you have done and are doing, for I am delighted. God bless you.

2. See that all the savings of the House you mention,2 for they are now finishing the building, and for the church, which is completed. I assure you it is fine, a true temple of the Lord; you will be truly pleased.3

3. My God! if you could see! Oh! what troubles we have! I have placed everything in Jesus, and he alone is everything for me! So pray and have others pray for me, for I need it so.

4. I hope to set out by the 22nd; if you have nothing urgent do not write, but pray; I am your affectionate M. ROSA

1. Your esteemed letter has reached me, and I reply promptly.1

2. I note what you say about the bed and am content that she should bring the equivalent sum.

3. There are none of the formalities you mention; let her come when she likes and bring the full dowry and trousseau on entering.2

4. I believe I have explained myself clearly; meanwhile please accept my respects; I sign myself your

most devoted servant Sister Anna ROSA GATTORNO

She tells her she will come to Florence.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. The devil wants to get in everywhere;1 I hope that when I come everything will be settled. Of course I am alone with Sr. A. Benedetta. I would certainly like you with me, all the more as I am not very well.2

2. I hope to be able to come by the 22nd, for I really need to leave; you will hear what is going on.3 Have others pray, for I need it. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is pleased with her expressions of trust and affection.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letter comforted me. Well done, my daughter; I never doubted your affection for your poor mother.1 Carry on, and you will truly be the comfort of all, especially of the one who in the heart of Jesus calls herself yours for all ages, in haste,

affectionate M. ROSA

She encloses a letter for a Sister in the hope that she will mend her ways.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply by return of post. Listen, give this letter of mine to the sister, and if she does not change, then we will see about changing her;1 but you must know I have no other qualified one, for all are [engaged]; enough; I am in a sea, an abyss of worries2 and work,

your affectionate M. ROSA

A.M.F.

My daughters,

1. I wish that, when your Superior is away from home, Sr. A. Veronica should take her place;2 respect her and obey her as if she were the Superior herself. I do not doubt that you will obey, and am sure of being heeded in everything; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

News of the journey, notes about postulants, and a request for a document.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I had a telegram sent, and you will have heard that the journey went well and nothing happened to me, though I certainly suffered.1 Now my headache has eased a little, but the pain! God's will be done.

2. I enclose postulants' letters; have this priest thanked, but not in my name, no, for they will tell him I am not there; you will see there is one from Ovada.

your affectionate M. ROSA

Send me at once the will I forgot in the left-hand drawer of the desk. Sew it securely inside Sr. A. Marcellina's bodice and send her here with the other one.

She tells her of one Sister's arrival and of another's temporary move to Pisa.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, you will receive Sr. A. Carenza, and put her in Sr. A. degli Angeli's place; but before she leaves give her a good little sermon: let her be good and do herself credit, not behave as she did here; tell her to be all for Jesus and not for creatures. I could say nothing to her, as I have to send her off without warning.1

2. If the one from cufo (?) wants to be clothed, so much the better, for then she could come here in Carenza's place. I hear you have received the money. Oh! if only the time had come to send it!2 Enough!

4. So, if you have held the clothing ceremony,4 or if there is one of the older ones who would be good for that house.5 Enough.

5. God willing, tomorrow at 8 I shall be in Pisa and stay there until Tuesday morning,6 when I will take the 6 o'clock from Pisa to Rome. God willing, I shall be in Rome that evening. For your information. Goodbye; it is late and I am tired. My health is the same as ever,

your affectionate M. ROSA

She tells her of the Sisters about to leave for America. She is in debt from building work, opening houses and running the Institute, and hopes for financial help from her.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. Since I have a moment — I am unwell in Florence on my way to Rome1 and am waiting for the sisters — I take the opportunity to write, so as to send this to the sisters in Genoa who are about to sail for your country;2 they will hand it to you themselves.

2. I hope you have by now handed everything over to the person I sent for the purpose;3 so think of me (who always), for you will see by deeds that I always think of you and of that house of yours. Oh! what troubles!

3. You will hear from Sr. A. Demetria — she is the pharmacist — what a dear sister! You can use her as you wish; she is an angel in the flesh, and she will tell you everything. She has a fine pharmacist's diploma; I assure you she is more of heaven than of earth.

4. The young qualified one, Sr. A. Stimatina — oh! what a dear creature, my God! I have deprived myself of truly observant and dear souls4 whom I formed with such effort, and what the diploma cost me! My God!

She seeks advice and help on a matter that grieves her: the ruling of the Congregation of B. and R. on the size of postulants' dowries (no less than £ 500). She sets out the harm this will do to young women and to the Institute, and submits for his judgment and support the petition she has prepared for the Congregation.1

Most Reverend Monsignor,

1. I know from experience how much you love this poor Institute and what consideration you show me, who feel too insignificant to deserve any regard at all; it is precisely relying on your charity and indulgence towards me that I turn to you, sure that the request I am about to make will be well received and that I shall be supported by your wise counsel. Ah! do not abandon me at this moment, when your help is so needed by this poor Institute.

2. I write to you in confidence about the decisions taken by the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars on the Holy Rules that govern this poor Institute. It is a daughter speaking to her kind father to learn from him how she should proceed, and in complete secrecy.

3. To the point, then: what the S. Congregation has ordered will be fully carried out by us. Only one point gives me much to think about and makes me very fearful: the one concerning the acceptance of postulants.2

4. That article prescribes a dowry of more than 500 lire, and the experience of many years has taught me that, if this is laid down, only three or four young women a òli year could be admitted to the Institute and no more, while we would be forced to turn away over a hundred who come with dowries of less than 500 lire.

5. I have listed the applications made this year with less than 500 lire, and they number about ninety.3 Are all these young women to be prevented from fulfilling their desires because they lack the prescribed dowry? And will the Institute, deprived of personnel, not soon die out?4

6. These considerations cause me too much pain, and I hope the Lord will find a remedy by allowing us to admit to the Institute those young women who, even with little or no dowry, have the qualities needed to become good and worthy Daughters of Saint Anne.

7. I have prepared a petition to the S. Congregation seeking an amendment to this article; but before presenting it I would like to hear your wise opinion.5

8. What great charity it would be for this poor Institute, and especially for me, if Your Most Reverend Excellency would deign to speak with the Most Reverend Secretary of the S. Congregation, with whom I know you are on close terms, to learn whether the petition I would present might be considered and not meet with the S. Congregation's disapproval!

9. You did me a similar favor in the time of poor Agnozzi,6 from whom you obtained favors I shall never forget. Do what you can this time too with the present secretary, by virtue of your friendship, so that the S. Congregation may find my reasons just and grant what I ask.

10. I await a venerated letter from you to console me, and meanwhile I am preparing a copy of the petition to send you, for I want you to see it before it is presented, so as to have your wise opinion.7

[Most humble and obedient Daughter] [Sister Anna ROSA GATTORNO]

Professing humble obedience, she sets out her observations on the article of the Constitutions concerning postulants' dowries, based on personal experience. She explains the Institute's administrative criteria and practices, which justify her request to amend the article.1

Most Venerable S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars

1. Filled with the deepest veneration for the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, to which I shall always be submissive and most obedient, knowing how worthy of respectful observance are the orders it sees fit to give in its immense wisdom and fairness, I have no words adequate to express the lively gratitude I feel for what it has done for this Institute, which will always remember with grateful heart such noble acts of sublime charity and will ever wish to see the Lord reward the great benefit received.

2. And now, encouraged by the S. Congregation's kindness and indulgence towards me, a poor sinner deserving nothing but the Lord's disapproval, I venture to present some observations on the article on dowries in the Holy Rules, the fruit of my own experience,2 commending myself to the S. Congregation's charity that they be regarded as unsaid should they not meet with its approval.

3. That article prescribes, save in exceptional cases, a dowry of more than five hundred lire, and that the dowry brought be reinvested in full.

4. On the first point I venture to observe that, if a dowry of more than 500 lire is required, the Institute will soon die out. The facts make this evident, and I can assure you that this year, of all the young women who applied to enter this Institute, I accepted only three, with a thousand lire, while I had to refuse very many applications (about ninety) from very robust young women who would have been a great help to the Institute and would have made excellent Daughters of Saint Anne, their applications being supported by excellent references, solely because their dowries were below five hundred lire.

5. In these times of general hardship and, let us say it, of coldness towards the things of God, very few families can or will give more than half a thousand lire to daughters who wish to become religious; hence these girls cannot fulfill their soul's desire to consecrate themselves to God's service and withdraw from a corrupt and vicious society to keep themselves pure and spotless within the walls of a cloister.3 Now, would not this number of people I had to refuse have wonderfully helped the Institute to grow?4 Is it not true that by the fruit of their work in Hospitals, Schools and elsewhere they would have made up for their small dowries, while the Institute could have taken on greater commitments: free home nursing of the sick, paid service in Hospitals, Asylums, Crèches and Homes for deaf-mute girls, and the instruction of children?

6. How will the Institute, with the three or four young women at most who will come each year with the dowry fixed by that article, replace the fifteen sisters who on average leave this earth of sorrows each year to enjoy Paradise, and those who through illness or old age become unable to work?

7. How can we accept the new houses that God in his mercy offers us if we lack personnel?

8. Moreover, the Institute needs nurses, for whom robust people are required, and these come from the countryside and from farming families who, even if comfortably off, can hardly provide nearly a thousand lire as a dowry for their daughters; note too that the dowry of the Daughters of Saint Anne is the work they do in exercising charity.

9. In view of these considerations, and in the sad conviction that, if a dowry of more than 500 lire were fixed, the Institute would be forced to close houses one by one for lack of personnel instead of increasing them, and so would soon die out, I appeal to the immensely great charity of the S. Congregation to deign to allow this Institute to accept those young women who have the necessary qualities and a firm and sincere vocation to become Daughters of Saint Anne, but who could not fulfill their desire because they lack the required dowry.5

10. As for reinvesting the dowry, whatever its size, I also venture (always in full submission to any decision the S. Congregation may wish to take) to point out the following.

11. As the S. Congregation well knows, many religious Corporations — for example the Salesian Sisters, the Sisters of Charity, those of the Sacred Heart, the Josephite Sisters and various others — charge those admitted a daily sum for board and all other necessary expenses during postulancy and novitiate.

12. So have we done hitherto, though limiting the daily charge to only one lira, in the interest of the young women themselves.6

13. During postulancy and novitiate the young women admitted, while preparing for the religious life they are to embrace, are of no help to the Institute, which must keep them permanently at the Mother House; that is why one lira a day is charged for the expenses incurred on their behalf.

14. This sum is taken from the dowry, and should any entrant wish to return to her family, or be sent back for legitimate reasons, what she brought to the Institute on entering is returned to her, less what was spent on her board and clothing — the former reckoned at as many lire as days she spent in the Institute, the latter at 150 lire.

15. The Franciscans too pay 200 lire for clothing, and we, as Tertiaries of St Francis, keep this custom; and as such we have lived hitherto on the Providence the Lord sends us through free home nursing, the salaries received by both hospital nurses and teachers, and alms-collecting.7

16. Yes, this is our chief means of subsistence; from it several of our houses draw what they need not only to support themselves, but with the surplus they can generously help the Mother

House and other sister houses. God protects the poor alms-collecting sisters, who are welcomed everywhere and receive generous help. 17. Thus, by adding to the yearly savings the portion of the dowry that is reinvested, the Institute already owns several houses, and it is to be hoped that, prospering more and more with the help of the Lord and of our glorious Mother Saint Anne, it may come to own other larger properties. In this the desire the S. Congregation expressed in framing that article will be fulfilled — the S. Congregation to which I shall always be submissive and most obedient,

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO
